description: Parts of Speech question bank derived from FDA & SDA Competitive Examination Notes. Covers Noun, Pronoun, Verb, Adjective, Adverb, Preposition, Conjunction, Interjection, Articles, words that change part of speech, high-frequency exam distinctions and error correction. Verify before formal examination use.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are parts of speech?

options.A: The classes into which words are grouped according to the work they perform in a sentence
options.B: The punctuation marks used in a sentence
options.D: The degrees of comparison of an adjective

questions.explanation: Parts of speech are the classes into which words are grouped according to the work they perform in a sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How many traditional parts of speech are commonly taught in English grammar?

options.A: Six

questions.explanation: There are eight traditional parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why must a word be judged by its function in a sentence?

options.A: Because all words have only one fixed part of speech
options.B: Because a word can perform different grammatical functions in different sentences
options.C: Because only nouns can change their part of speech
options.D: Because function is decided only by spelling

questions.explanation: A word can perform different grammatical functions in different sentences; for example, work is a noun in 'My work is complete' and a verb in 'I work every day.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a sentence?

options.A: A group of words that expresses a complete thought and normally contains a subject and a finite verb
options.B: A group of words without a verb
options.D: A phrase that cannot stand alone

questions.explanation: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought and normally contains a subject and a finite verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the subject of a sentence?

options.A: The part that contains the verb and its objects
options.B: The person, thing or idea that the sentence is about, or the one that performs or experiences the action
options.C: The punctuation at the end of the sentence

questions.explanation: The subject is the person, thing or idea that the sentence is about, or the one that performs or experiences the action.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the predicate of a sentence?

options.A: The part that says something about the subject and contains the verb
options.B: The first word of the sentence
options.C: The noun phrase that acts as subject

questions.explanation: The predicate is the part of a sentence that says something about the subject; it contains the verb and may include its objects and complements.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a noun?

options.A: A word used to name a person, place, animal, thing, substance, quality, state, action or idea
options.B: A word that modifies a verb
options.D: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: A noun is a word used to name a person, place, animal, thing, substance, quality, state, action or idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an abstract noun?

options.A: Table

questions.explanation: Honesty names a quality that cannot usually be perceived through the five senses, so it is an abstract noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a proper noun?

options.A: A noun that names a class or kind of person, place or thing
options.B: The particular name of a specific person, place, institution, day, month, book or other unique entity
options.C: A noun that names a group considered as a unit
options.D: A noun that names a substance or material

questions.explanation: A proper noun is the particular name of a specific person, place, institution, day, month, book or other unique entity and normally begins with a capital letter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a proper noun?

options.A: boy

questions.explanation: Karnataka is the particular name of a specific place and is a proper noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a common noun?

options.A: A noun that names a class or kind of person, place or thing rather than a particular individual
options.B: A noun that names a specific person or place
options.C: A noun that names a group as a unit
options.D: A noun that cannot be counted

questions.explanation: A common noun names a class or kind of person, place or thing rather than a particular individual, such as boy, city, state, river, school.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a collective noun?

options.A: A noun that names a substance or material
options.B: A noun that names a group considered as a unit
options.C: A noun that names a quality or feeling
options.D: A noun that can be counted

questions.explanation: A collective noun names a group considered as a unit, such as team, committee, jury, flock, herd, bunch, audience.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a collective noun?

options.A: gold

questions.explanation: Committee names a group considered as a unit and is a collective noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a material noun?

options.A: A noun that names a group as a unit
options.B: A noun that names a substance or material from which things are made
options.C: A noun that names a quality or idea
options.D: A noun that names a specific person

questions.explanation: A material noun names a substance or material from which things are made, such as gold, silver, water, cotton, iron, wood.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a material noun?

options.A: beauty

questions.explanation: Cotton names a substance or material and is a material noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an abstract noun?

options.A: A noun that names something perceived through the five senses
options.B: A noun that names a quality, feeling, condition, state or idea that cannot usually be perceived through the five senses
options.C: A noun that names a group as a unit
options.D: A noun that names a specific place

questions.explanation: An abstract noun names a quality, feeling, condition, state or idea that cannot usually be perceived through the five senses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a concrete noun?

options.A: happiness

questions.explanation: A concrete noun names something that can be perceived through one or more senses; mango can be seen, touched and tasted.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a countable noun?

options.A: A noun that refers to something that can be counted and has singular and plural forms
options.B: A noun that is always plural
options.C: A noun that cannot be counted
options.D: A noun that names a material only

questions.explanation: A countable noun refers to something that can be counted and has singular and plural forms, such as one book, two books.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an uncountable noun?

options.A: A noun that has both singular and plural forms
options.B: A noun that refers to something not normally counted as separate units
options.C: A noun that names a specific person
options.D: A noun that names a group as a unit

questions.explanation: An uncountable noun refers to something not normally counted as separate units, such as information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment, water.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an uncountable noun?

options.A: book

questions.explanation: Information is not normally counted as separate units and is an uncountable noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can an abstract noun be countable?

options.A: No, all abstract nouns are uncountable
options.B: Yes, some abstract nouns are countable, such as an idea, two ideas
options.C: Yes, but only proper nouns are countable
options.D: No, abstract nouns have no plural form

questions.explanation: Some abstract nouns are countable, such as an idea, two ideas; a belief, several beliefs. Others are usually uncountable, such as honesty and information.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the singular number of a noun?

options.A: The form that denotes more than one
options.B: The form that denotes one person or thing
options.C: The form that denotes a group
options.D: The form that denotes a material

questions.explanation: The singular form denotes one person or thing, for example book, child, woman.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the usual rule for forming regular plurals?

options.A: Add -es to all nouns
options.C: Change the vowel in the noun

questions.explanation: Most nouns form the plural by adding -s: book-books, pen-pens.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is -es added to form a plural?

options.A: Nouns ending in vowel + y
options.B: Nouns ending in sounds or letters such as -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x and often -z

questions.explanation: Nouns ending in sounds or letters such as -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x and often -z generally take -es: bus-buses, class-classes, brush-brushes, watch-watches, box-boxes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How do many nouns ending in consonant + y form the plural?

options.A: The y changes to ies

questions.explanation: Many nouns ending in consonant + y change the y to ies: city-cities, baby-babies.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How do nouns ending in vowel + y form the plural?

options.A: They change y to ies

questions.explanation: Nouns ending in vowel + y generally add -s: boy-boys, key-keys, day-days.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How do many nouns ending in -f or -fe form the plural?

options.A: All change -f/-fe to -ves
options.B: Some change -f/-fe to -ves, but this is not universal

questions.explanation: Some change -f/-fe to -ves: leaf-leaves, wife-wives, knife-knives. However, this is not universal: roof-roofs, belief-beliefs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are irregular plurals?

options.A: Plurals formed by adding -s
options.B: Plurals that do not follow the usual -s/-es pattern

questions.explanation: Irregular plurals do not follow the usual -s/-es pattern, such as man-men, woman-women, child-children, tooth-teeth, foot-feet, mouse-mice, goose-geese.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'child'?

options.A: childs

questions.explanation: Child is an irregular plural: child-children.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'tooth'?

options.A: tooths

questions.explanation: Tooth is an irregular plural: tooth-teeth.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which nouns have the same singular and plural forms?

options.A: sheep, deer, species, series

questions.explanation: Examples include sheep, deer, species, series. Context determines whether the meaning is singular or plural.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are plural-only nouns?

options.A: Nouns that are normally used in the plural, such as scissors, trousers, spectacles, goods
options.C: Nouns that have no plural form
options.D: Nouns that change meaning when singular

questions.explanation: Plural-only nouns are normally used in the plural, such as scissors, trousers, spectacles, goods. They usually take a plural verb, but a pair of takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is correct?

options.A: A pair of scissors are on the desk.
options.B: A pair of scissors is on the desk.
options.C: A pair of scissors were on the desk.
options.D: A pair of scissors have on the desk.

questions.explanation: Plural-only nouns usually take a plural verb, but a pair of takes a singular verb: 'A pair of scissors is on the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair shows a noun that changes meaning when pluralised?

options.A: book-books

questions.explanation: Some nouns change meaning when pluralised. Examples: custom-customs (habit-duties/taxes), manner-manners (method-social behaviour), work-works (employment-literary or artistic creations).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is grammatical gender in English?

options.A: A grammatical classification traditionally expressed as masculine, feminine, common or neuter

questions.explanation: Gender is a grammatical classification traditionally expressed as masculine, feminine, common or neuter in English.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is in the masculine gender?

options.A: queen

questions.explanation: Masculine gender denotes a male person or animal in traditional classification, for example man, king, bull.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is in the feminine gender?

options.A: bull

questions.explanation: Feminine gender denotes a female person or animal in traditional classification, for example woman, queen, cow.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is in the common gender?

options.A: teacher

questions.explanation: Common gender refers to a person or animal whose sex is not specified or whose gender is not grammatically marked, for example teacher, doctor, student, child.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is in the neuter gender?

options.A: man

questions.explanation: Neuter gender traditionally refers to things without biological sex, for example table, stone, book.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the possessive case of a singular noun usually formed?

options.A: Apostrophe + s

questions.explanation: A singular noun usually takes apostrophe + s: the girl's bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the possessive of a regular plural ending in -s usually formed?

options.A: Add apostrophe + s

questions.explanation: A regular plural ending in -s usually takes an apostrophe: the girls' bags.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is the possessive of an irregular plural formed?

options.A: Add only an apostrophe

questions.explanation: Add apostrophe + s for irregular plurals: children's books, men's clothes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a noun phrase?

options.A: A group of words built around a noun or pronoun and functioning as a noun unit
options.B: A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb
options.C: A word that replaces a noun
options.D: A word that modifies a verb

questions.explanation: A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun or pronoun and functioning as a noun unit, such as 'The tall boy in the blue shirt'.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a gerund used as a noun?

options.A: The -ed form of a verb used as a noun
options.B: The -ing form of a verb used as a noun
options.C: The base form of a verb used as a noun
options.D: The past participle used as a noun

questions.explanation: A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun, as in 'Swimming is good exercise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a verbal noun?

options.A: A noun formed from a verb and used as a noun, often naming an action or result
options.B: A verb formed from a noun
options.C: An adjective formed from a verb

questions.explanation: A verbal noun is a noun formed from a verb and used as a noun, often naming an action or result, such as arrival, decision, movement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following nouns is commonly uncountable in examination questions?

options.A: book

questions.explanation: Common uncountable nouns in examination questions include advice, information, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, knowledge, scenery, bread, traffic.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which expression is correct?

options.A: an advice

questions.explanation: Do not normally write an advice or informations; use a piece of advice and pieces of information.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'criterion'?

options.A: criterions

questions.explanation: The plural of criterion is criteria.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'phenomenon'?

options.A: phenomenons

questions.explanation: The plural of phenomenon is phenomena.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'analysis'?

options.A: analysiss

questions.explanation: The plural of analysis is analyses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'basis'?

options.A: basises

questions.explanation: The plural of basis is bases.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'thesis'?

options.A: thesises

questions.explanation: The plural of thesis is theses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'crisis'?

options.A: crisises

questions.explanation: The plural of crisis is crises.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'syllabus'?

options.A: syllabuses or syllabi

questions.explanation: The plural of syllabus is syllabuses or syllabi; both are used.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'medium'?

options.A: medias
options.B: media in many contexts; mediums is also used for people who claim to communicate with spirits or for individual means/methods

questions.explanation: The plural of medium is media in many contexts; mediums is also used for people who claim to communicate with spirits or for individual means/methods.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'datum'?

options.A: datums only
options.B: data; in modern usage, data is also frequently treated as a mass singular noun, depending on context and style

questions.explanation: The plural of datum is data; in modern usage, data is also frequently treated as a mass singular noun, depending on context and style.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a pronoun?

options.A: A word used instead of a noun or noun phrase, usually to avoid repetition
options.B: A word that names a person or place
options.C: A word that modifies a verb

questions.explanation: A pronoun is a word used instead of a noun or noun phrase, usually to avoid repetition, as in 'Meena is absent because she is ill.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an antecedent?

options.A: The noun or noun phrase to which a pronoun refers
options.B: The verb that follows a pronoun

questions.explanation: An antecedent is the noun or noun phrase to which a pronoun refers. In 'Ravi lost his pen,' Ravi is the antecedent of his.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a personal pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that refers to a particular person or thing
options.B: A pronoun that asks a question
options.C: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.D: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship

questions.explanation: A personal pronoun refers to a particular person or thing; forms include I, me, we, us, you, he, him, she, her, it, they, them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are subject forms of personal pronouns?

options.A: me, us, him, her, them
options.B: I, we, you, he, she, it, they
options.C: mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs

questions.explanation: The subject forms are I, we, you, he, she, it, they. Example: 'She teaches English.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are object forms of personal pronouns?

options.A: I, we, you, he, she, it, they
options.B: me, us, you, him, her, it, them
options.C: mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs

questions.explanation: The object forms are me, us, you, him, her, it, them. Example: 'The teacher praised him.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are possessive pronouns?

options.A: Pronouns that show ownership and stand independently: mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs
options.B: Pronouns that come before nouns: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
options.C: Pronouns that refer back to the subject

questions.explanation: Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand independently: mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs. Example: 'This book is mine.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are possessive determiners different from possessive pronouns?

options.A: Possessive determiners come before nouns, while possessive pronouns replace the noun phrase
options.B: Possessive determiners replace the noun phrase, while possessive pronouns come before nouns
options.D: Possessive pronouns come before nouns, while determiners stand alone

questions.explanation: Possessive determiners come before nouns (my book, their house), while possessive pronouns replace the noun phrase (the book is mine; the house is theirs).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a reflexive pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that refers back to the subject when the subject and object are the same person or thing
options.B: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.C: A pronoun that asks a question
options.D: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject when the subject and object are the same person or thing: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?

options.A: She blamed herself.

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject: 'She blamed herself.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an emphatic or intensive pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that emphasises a noun or pronoun and can be removed without making the basic sentence grammatically incomplete
options.B: A pronoun that is required to complete the meaning of the sentence
options.C: A pronoun that asks a question
options.D: A pronoun that points to a person or thing

questions.explanation: An emphatic pronoun emphasises a noun or pronoun and can be removed without making the basic sentence grammatically incomplete, as in 'The principal herself addressed the students.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How can reflexive and emphatic pronouns be distinguished?

options.A: A reflexive pronoun is required to complete the intended meaning when it is the object; an emphatic pronoun merely adds emphasis
options.B: A reflexive pronoun merely adds emphasis; an emphatic pronoun is required
options.D: Reflexive pronouns come before nouns; emphatic pronouns come after verbs

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is required to complete the intended meaning when it is the object ('He hurt himself'); an emphatic pronoun merely adds emphasis ('He himself opened the gate').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a demonstrative pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that points to a person or thing: this, that, these, those
options.B: A pronoun that asks a question
options.C: A pronoun that refers back to the subject
options.D: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship

questions.explanation: A demonstrative pronoun points to a person or thing: this, that, these, those. Example: 'These are expensive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How do this/that differ from these/those?

options.A: This and that are singular; these and those are plural
options.B: This and these are singular; that and those are plural
options.C: This and that are plural; these and those are singular

questions.explanation: This and that are singular; these and those are plural. This/these generally indicate nearness; that/those generally indicate distance.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an interrogative pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun used to ask a question: who, whom, whose, which, what
options.B: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.C: A pronoun that refers back to the subject
options.D: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship

questions.explanation: An interrogative pronoun is used to ask a question: who, whom, whose, which, what. Example: 'Who called you?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'who' used and when is 'whom' used?

options.A: Who is the subject form; whom is the object form
options.B: Who is the object form; whom is the subject form
options.C: Who is used for things; whom is used for people
options.D: They are always interchangeable in formal English

questions.explanation: Who is the subject form ('Who came?'); whom is the object form ('Whom did you meet?'). In informal English, who is often used instead of whom.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a relative pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that introduces a relative clause and relates it to a noun or pronoun: who, whom, whose, which, that
options.B: A pronoun that asks a question
options.C: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.D: A pronoun that refers back to the subject

questions.explanation: A relative pronoun introduces a relative clause and relates it to a noun or pronoun: who, whom, whose, which, that. Example: 'The woman who won the prize is my teacher.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'who' used as a relative pronoun?

options.A: Who generally refers to people and functions as the subject of the relative clause
options.B: Who generally refers to things and functions as the object

questions.explanation: Who generally refers to people and functions as the subject of the relative clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'whom' used as a relative pronoun?

options.A: Whom generally refers to people and functions as the object of the relative clause
options.B: Whom generally refers to things and functions as the subject

questions.explanation: Whom generally refers to people and functions as the object of the relative clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'whose' used?

options.A: Whose expresses possession and can refer to people and, in formal usage, sometimes things
options.C: Whose is used only to ask questions

questions.explanation: Whose expresses possession and can refer to people and, in formal usage, sometimes things. Example: 'The student whose bag was missing reported it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'which' used as a relative pronoun?

options.A: Which generally refers to animals or things and can introduce defining or non-defining relative clauses
options.B: Which generally refers to people only
options.D: Which is used only to ask questions

questions.explanation: Which generally refers to animals or things. It can introduce defining or non-defining relative clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'that' used as a relative pronoun?

options.A: That commonly introduces defining relative clauses referring to people, animals or things; it is not normally used after a comma in a non-defining clause
options.B: That is used only in non-defining clauses
options.D: That is used only to ask questions

questions.explanation: That commonly introduces defining relative clauses referring to people, animals or things; it is not normally used after a comma in a non-defining clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an indefinite pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that refers to a person or thing without identifying it exactly
options.B: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.C: A pronoun that asks a question
options.D: A pronoun that refers back to the subject

questions.explanation: An indefinite pronoun refers to a person or thing without identifying it exactly. Examples: someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, everyone, everybody, no one, nothing, something, few, many, several, all, some, none.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Do indefinite pronouns always take singular verbs?

options.A: Yes, all indefinite pronouns take singular verbs
options.B: No; everybody, everyone, somebody, anyone, each, either, neither normally take singular verbs, but both, few, many, several take plural verbs, and all, some, any, none depend on the noun or meaning
options.C: No; all indefinite pronouns take plural verbs

questions.explanation: Everybody, everyone, somebody, anyone, each, either, neither normally take singular verbs; both, few, many, several take plural verbs. All, some, any, none depend on the noun or meaning they refer to.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a distributive pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that refers to members of a group individually: each, either, neither
options.B: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship
options.C: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.D: A pronoun that asks a question

questions.explanation: A distributive pronoun refers to members of a group individually: each, either, neither. These normally take singular verbs when used as pronouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a reciprocal pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship: each other and one another
options.B: A pronoun that refers back to the subject
options.C: A pronoun that points to a person or thing
options.D: A pronoun that asks a question

questions.explanation: A reciprocal pronoun expresses a mutual relationship. The forms are each other and one another. Example: 'The two friends help each other.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a substitute or prop pronoun?

options.A: A pronoun that stands in place of a previously mentioned noun or noun phrase, preventing repetition
options.B: A pronoun that asks a question
options.C: A pronoun that expresses a mutual relationship
options.D: A pronoun that refers back to the subject

questions.explanation: A substitute pronoun stands in place of a previously mentioned noun or noun phrase, preventing repetition. Example: 'I prefer the red shirt; do you have one?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is pronoun-antecedent agreement?

options.A: A pronoun should agree with its antecedent in number and, where relevant, person and gender
options.B: A pronoun should always be singular
options.C: A pronoun should always be plural
options.D: A pronoun should never refer to a noun

questions.explanation: A pronoun should agree with its antecedent in number and, where relevant, person and gender. Example: 'The girls brought their books.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which verb is used after each, either and neither when they are subjects?

options.A: A plural verb
options.C: Either singular or plural without any rule

questions.explanation: They normally take a singular verb: 'Each of the boys is ready'; 'Neither answer is correct.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pronoun is preferred after a preposition in formal standard English?

options.A: The subject form

questions.explanation: The object form is used after a preposition: between you and me, not between you and I.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct form?

options.A: Myself and Ravi went.

questions.explanation: 'Ravi and I went' is correct because the pronoun is part of the subject. Myself should not normally replace I as an ordinary subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct form?

options.A: The teacher called Rani and I.
options.B: The teacher called Rani and me.
options.C: The teacher called Rani and myself.
options.D: The teacher called I and Rani.

questions.explanation: 'The teacher called Rani and me' is correct because the pronoun is the object of called.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'few' and 'a few'?

options.A: Few means almost none and has a negative sense; a few means some and has a positive sense
options.B: Few means some; a few means almost none
options.D: Few is used with uncountable nouns only

questions.explanation: Few means almost none and has a negative sense; a few means some and has a positive sense. Example: 'Few students understood' versus 'A few students understood.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'little' and 'a little'?

options.A: Little means almost no amount; a little means some amount
options.B: Little means some amount; a little means almost no amount
options.D: Little is used with countable nouns only

questions.explanation: Little means almost no amount; a little means some amount. Example: 'There is little hope' versus 'There is a little hope.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'each' and 'every'?

options.A: Each emphasises individuals separately; every refers to all members of a group collectively while considering them individually
options.B: Each refers to groups; every emphasises individuals separately
options.C: Both are used only with plural nouns
options.D: Every is used only with uncountable nouns

questions.explanation: Each emphasises individuals separately; every refers to all members of a group collectively while considering them individually. Both normally take singular nouns and singular verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'some' and 'any'?

options.A: Some is common in affirmative statements and offers/requests expecting a positive response; any is common in negatives and questions
options.B: Some is common in negatives; any is common in affirmative statements
options.C: Both are used only in questions
options.D: Any is used only in affirmative statements

questions.explanation: Some is common in affirmative statements and offers/requests expecting a positive response; any is common in negatives and questions, and can mean 'whichever' in affirmative sentences.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the main verb or lexical verb?

options.A: The verb that carries the central meaning of the verb phrase
options.B: The verb that helps another verb form tense
options.C: The verb that connects the subject to a complement
options.D: The verb that takes two objects

questions.explanation: The main verb carries the central meaning of the verb phrase. Example: 'They play cricket.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an auxiliary or helping verb?

options.A: A verb that helps the main verb form tense, voice, questions, negatives or emphasis
options.B: The verb that carries the central meaning
options.C: A verb that takes a direct object
options.D: A verb that does not take a direct object

questions.explanation: An auxiliary verb helps the main verb form tense, voice, questions, negatives or emphasis. Primary auxiliaries are be, have, do; modal auxiliaries include can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the primary auxiliaries?

options.A: Can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must
options.B: Be (am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been), have (have, has, had) and do (do, does, did)

questions.explanation: The primary auxiliaries are be (am, is, are, was, were, be, being, been), have (have, has, had) and do (do, does, did).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are modal auxiliary verbs?

options.A: Verbs that express meanings such as ability, possibility, permission, obligation, advice, prediction or willingness
options.B: Verbs that carry the central meaning of the verb phrase
options.D: Verbs that do not show tense

questions.explanation: Modals express meanings such as ability, possibility, permission, obligation, advice, prediction or willingness. Common modals are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a finite verb?

options.A: A verb marked for tense and/or agreement with the subject that can serve as the main verb of an independent clause
options.B: A verb that does not show tense or subject agreement
options.C: A verb that takes two objects
options.D: A verb that does not take a direct object

questions.explanation: A finite verb is marked for tense and/or agreement with the subject and can serve as the main verb of an independent clause. Example: 'She works here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a non-finite verb?

options.A: A verb form that does not show tense or subject agreement by itself; main forms are infinitives, gerunds and participles
options.B: A verb marked for tense and agreement with the subject
options.C: A verb that takes a direct object
options.D: A verb that takes an indirect object

questions.explanation: A non-finite verb form does not show tense or subject agreement by itself. The main forms are infinitives, gerunds and participles. Examples: to read, reading, written.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a transitive verb?

options.A: A verb that takes a direct object
options.B: A verb that does not take a direct object
options.C: A verb that connects the subject to a complement
options.D: A verb that takes two objects

questions.explanation: A transitive verb takes a direct object. Example: 'She opened the door.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an intransitive verb?

options.A: A verb that takes a direct object
options.B: A verb that does not take a direct object
options.C: A verb that connects the subject to a complement
options.D: A verb that takes two objects

questions.explanation: An intransitive verb does not take a direct object. Example: 'The baby slept.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a verb be both transitive and intransitive?

options.A: No, a verb is always either transitive or intransitive
options.B: Yes, its use depends on the sentence
options.C: Only auxiliary verbs can be both
options.D: Only linking verbs can be both

questions.explanation: Yes, a verb can be both. Its use depends on the sentence: 'She reads every day' (intransitive use) and 'She reads a novel' (transitive use).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a ditransitive verb?

options.A: A verb that takes a direct object only
options.B: A verb that can take an indirect object and a direct object
options.C: A verb that takes no object
options.D: A verb that connects the subject to a complement

questions.explanation: A ditransitive verb can take an indirect object and a direct object. Example: 'He gave me a pen.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a linking verb?

options.A: A verb that connects the subject to a subject complement that describes or identifies it
options.B: A verb that takes two objects
options.C: A verb that takes no subject
options.D: A verb that helps form questions

questions.explanation: A linking verb connects the subject to a subject complement that describes or identifies it. Common linking verbs include forms of be and verbs such as seem, become, appear, feel, look, smell, taste when they express a state. Example: 'The soup tastes delicious.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a regular verb?

options.A: A verb that forms its simple past and past participle by adding -ed or -d
options.B: A verb that does not follow the -ed pattern
options.C: A verb that takes two objects
options.D: A verb that does not take a direct object

questions.explanation: A regular verb forms its simple past and past participle by adding -ed or -d. Examples: work-worked-worked; live-lived-lived.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an irregular verb?

options.A: A verb that forms its past and past participle by adding -ed
options.B: A verb that does not form its past and past participle by the regular -ed pattern
options.C: A verb that takes no object
options.D: A verb that connects the subject to a complement

questions.explanation: An irregular verb does not form its past and past participle by the regular -ed pattern. Examples: go-went-gone; write-wrote-written; see-saw-seen.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a phrasal verb?

options.A: A combination of a verb and one or more particles that functions as a unit
options.B: A verb that takes two objects
options.C: A verb that connects the subject to a complement
options.D: A verb that does not show tense

questions.explanation: A phrasal verb is a combination of a verb and one or more particles (adverbs or prepositions) that functions as a unit. Examples: give up (quit), look after (care for), put off (postpone), carry out (perform).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an infinitive?

options.A: The base form of a verb, commonly preceded by to
options.B: The -ing form used as a noun
options.C: The third principal form of a verb
options.D: The -ing form used in progressive verb phrases

questions.explanation: An infinitive is the base form of a verb, commonly preceded by to: to read, to write. A bare infinitive appears without to after many modal verbs and certain verbs: 'She can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a gerund?

options.A: An -ing verb form functioning as a noun
options.B: The base form of a verb preceded by to
options.C: The third principal form of a verb
options.D: An -ing form used only in progressive verb phrases

questions.explanation: A gerund is an -ing verb form functioning as a noun. Example: 'Reading improves vocabulary.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a present participle?

options.A: The -ing form used in progressive verb phrases or as an adjective
options.B: The third principal form of a verb
options.C: The base form preceded by to
options.D: The -ing form used only as a noun

questions.explanation: A present participle is the -ing form used in progressive verb phrases or as an adjective. Examples: 'She is reading'; 'the boiling water.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a past participle?

options.A: The third principal form of a verb, used in perfect tenses, passive constructions and adjective-like uses
options.B: The -ing form used as a noun
options.C: The base form preceded by to
options.D: The -ing form used in progressive phrases

questions.explanation: A past participle is the third principal form of a verb, used in perfect tenses, passive constructions and adjective-like uses. Examples: written, broken, gone, finished.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is a gerund different from a present participle?

options.A: A gerund functions as a noun; a present participle forms a progressive verb or modifies a noun
options.B: A gerund forms a progressive verb; a present participle functions as a noun
options.C: A gerund is the past participle; a present participle is the base form

questions.explanation: Both end in -ing. A gerund functions as a noun ('Swimming is healthy'); a present participle forms a progressive verb ('She is swimming') or modifies a noun ('the swimming child').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is tense?

options.A: The grammatical marking of time in a verb phrase

questions.explanation: Tense is the grammatical marking of time in a verb phrase. Traditional school grammar commonly teaches three broad time categories—present, past and future—and twelve tense patterns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the three principal forms of a verb?

options.A: The base form, simple past form and past participle form
options.B: The present, past and future forms
options.C: The infinitive, gerund and participle forms
options.D: The singular, plural and possessive forms

questions.explanation: The three principal forms of a verb are the base form, simple past form and past participle form. Example: write-wrote-written.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the simple present tense used for?

options.A: Habits, routines, general truths, facts and scheduled events
options.D: Actions completed before another past action

questions.explanation: The simple present tense is used for habits, routines, general truths, facts and scheduled events. Example: 'The earth revolves around the Sun.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the present continuous tense?

options.A: am/is/are + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The present continuous tense is used for actions happening now, temporary situations and arranged future events. Form: am/is/are + verb-ing. Example: 'She is studying.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the present perfect tense?

options.A: has/have + past participle

questions.explanation: The present perfect tense links a past action or experience to the present. Form: has/have + past participle. Example: 'I have completed the work.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the present perfect continuous tense?

options.A: has/have been + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous tense emphasises an action that began in the past and continues up to the present or has a present result. Form: has/have been + verb-ing. Example: 'They have been waiting for an hour.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the simple past tense used for?

options.A: A completed action or state in the past
options.C: An action that will happen in the future
options.D: An action completed before another past action

questions.explanation: The simple past tense describes a completed action or state in the past. Example: 'She visited Mysuru yesterday.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the past continuous tense?

options.A: was/were + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The past continuous tense describes an action in progress at a particular past time or an ongoing action interrupted by another. Form: was/were + verb-ing. Example: 'I was reading when he called.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the past perfect tense?

options.A: had + past participle

questions.explanation: The past perfect tense indicates an action completed before another past action or time. Form: had + past participle. Example: 'The train had left before we arrived.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the past perfect continuous tense?

options.A: had been + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous tense emphasises the duration of an action continuing up to a point in the past. Form: had been + verb-ing. Example: 'She had been working for two hours before the meeting began.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the simple future tense?

options.A: will + base verb

questions.explanation: The simple future tense commonly expresses a future prediction, decision or willingness. Form: will + base verb. Example: 'I will call you tomorrow.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the future continuous tense?

options.A: will be + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The future continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at a particular future time. Form: will be + verb-ing. Example: 'At 8 p.m., I will be studying.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the future perfect tense?

options.A: will have + past participle

questions.explanation: The future perfect tense describes an action that will be completed before a specified future time. Form: will have + past participle. Example: 'By Monday, she will have finished the report.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the form of the future perfect continuous tense?

options.A: will have been + verb-ing

questions.explanation: The future perfect continuous tense emphasises the duration of an action up to a specified future point. Form: will have been + verb-ing. Example: 'By June, he will have been working here for ten years.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is subject-verb agreement?

options.A: The verb must agree with its subject in person and number
options.B: The verb must always be plural
options.C: The verb must always be singular
options.D: The verb must agree with the object

questions.explanation: The verb must agree with its subject in person and number. Example: 'He works'; 'They work.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with two subjects joined by 'and'?

options.A: A plural verb is normally used, but a single idea or fixed unit may take a singular verb
options.B: A singular verb is always used
options.D: The verb agrees with the object

questions.explanation: A plural verb is normally used: 'Ravi and Rani are ready.' A single idea or a fixed unit may take a singular verb: 'Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens when two singular subjects are joined by either...or or neither...nor?

options.A: The verb generally agrees with the nearer subject
options.B: The verb always takes the plural form
options.C: The verb always takes the singular form
options.D: The verb agrees with the first subject only

questions.explanation: The verb generally agrees with the nearer subject. Example: 'Neither the teacher nor the students are ready'; 'Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with each, every, either and neither as the subject?

options.A: A plural verb
options.D: Either singular or plural without rule

questions.explanation: A singular verb is normally used: 'Every student has a book.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does a phrase between the subject and verb change agreement?

options.A: Yes, the verb agrees with the noun in the intervening phrase
options.B: No, the verb agrees with the grammatical subject, not with a noun inside an intervening phrase

questions.explanation: No. The verb agrees with the grammatical subject, not with a noun inside an intervening phrase. Example: 'The list of items is on the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with collective nouns?

options.A: A singular verb when the group is viewed as one unit; plural agreement may occur in British usage when members are viewed individually
options.C: Always a singular verb in all varieties

questions.explanation: A collective noun can take a singular verb when the group is viewed as one unit; plural agreement may occur in British usage when members are viewed individually. Example: 'The committee has reached its decision.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with news, mathematics and physics when they name a subject or field?

options.A: A plural verb

questions.explanation: They normally take a singular verb: 'The news is encouraging'; 'Mathematics is difficult.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What verb is used with 'a pair of scissors' or 'a pair of trousers'?

options.A: A plural verb

questions.explanation: The expression a pair of takes a singular verb: 'A pair of trousers is missing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'lie' and 'lay'?

options.A: Lie (recline) is intransitive; lay (put something down) is transitive and takes an object
options.B: Lie is transitive; lay is intransitive

questions.explanation: Lie (recline) is intransitive: lie-lay-lain. Lay (put something down) is transitive and takes an object: lay-laid-laid. Example: 'I lie down'; 'Lay the book on the table.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'rise' and 'raise'?

options.A: Rise is generally intransitive (move upwards); raise is transitive (lift something)
options.B: Rise is transitive; raise is intransitive

questions.explanation: Rise is generally intransitive and means move upwards: rise-rose-risen. Raise is transitive and means lift something: raise-raised-raised.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'sit' and 'set'?

options.A: Sit means take a seated position and normally has no object; set means put or place something and takes an object
options.B: Sit is transitive; set is intransitive

questions.explanation: Sit means take a seated position and normally has no object: sit-sat-sat. Set means put or place something and takes an object: set-set-set.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'borrow' and 'lend'?

options.A: Borrow means take something temporarily from someone; lend means give something temporarily to someone
options.B: Borrow means give something temporarily; lend means take something temporarily
options.D: Borrow is used only for money

questions.explanation: Borrow means take something temporarily from someone; lend means give something temporarily to someone. Example: 'May I borrow your pen?'; 'Can you lend me your pen?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'say' and 'tell'?

options.A: Say focuses on the words spoken and does not normally take a personal object directly without 'to'; tell commonly takes a person as object
options.B: Say always takes a personal object; tell never takes a personal object
options.D: Tell focuses on the words spoken; say takes a person as object

questions.explanation: Say focuses on the words spoken and does not normally take a personal object directly without to; tell commonly takes a person as object. Examples: 'She said that she was tired'; 'She told me that she was tired.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adjective?

options.A: A word that modifies or describes a noun or pronoun by giving information about quality, size, colour, number, amount, origin or other characteristics
options.B: A word that modifies a verb
options.D: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective is a word that modifies or describes a noun or pronoun by giving information about quality, size, colour, number, amount, origin or other characteristics. Examples: honest, tall, red, three, much.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which questions can an adjective answer?

options.A: What kind? Which one? How many? How much? Whose?

questions.explanation: An adjective can answer questions such as What kind? Which one? How many? How much? Whose?

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an attributive adjective?

options.A: An adjective that appears before the noun it modifies
options.B: An adjective that appears after a linking verb
options.C: An adjective that follows the noun it modifies
options.D: An adjective that modifies a verb

questions.explanation: An attributive adjective appears before the noun it modifies. Example: 'a beautiful garden.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a predicative adjective?

options.A: An adjective that appears after a linking verb and describes the subject
options.B: An adjective that appears before the noun it modifies
options.C: An adjective that follows the noun it modifies
options.D: An adjective that modifies a verb

questions.explanation: A predicative adjective appears after a linking verb and describes the subject. Example: 'The garden is beautiful.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a postpositive adjective?

options.A: An adjective that follows the noun or pronoun it modifies, often in fixed expressions or formal usage
options.B: An adjective that appears before the noun it modifies
options.C: An adjective that appears after a linking verb
options.D: An adjective that modifies a verb

questions.explanation: A postpositive adjective follows the noun or pronoun it modifies, often in fixed expressions or formal usage. Example: 'something useful'; 'the people responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adjective of quality?

options.A: An adjective that describes the nature or quality of a noun
options.B: An adjective that indicates an amount of an uncountable noun
options.C: An adjective that indicates number or order
options.D: An adjective that points out a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective of quality describes the nature or quality of a noun. Examples: brave soldier, honest person, difficult question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adjective of quantity?

options.A: An adjective that indicates an amount of an uncountable noun
options.B: An adjective that describes the quality of a noun
options.C: An adjective that indicates number or order
options.D: An adjective that points out a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective of quantity indicates an amount of an uncountable noun. Examples: some water, little milk, enough food, much time.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adjective of number?

options.A: An adjective that indicates number or order
options.B: An adjective that indicates an amount of an uncountable noun
options.C: An adjective that describes the quality of a noun
options.D: An adjective that points out a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective of number indicates number or order. Examples: three books, several students, first prize, many people.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a demonstrative adjective or determiner?

options.A: An adjective that points out a noun: this book, that house, these flowers, those trees
options.B: An adjective that indicates possession before a noun
options.C: An adjective that introduces a question before a noun
options.D: An adjective that refers to members of a group individually

questions.explanation: A demonstrative adjective or determiner points out a noun: this book, that house, these flowers, those trees. In modern grammar these words are usually called demonstrative determiners when they accompany nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a possessive adjective or determiner?

options.A: An adjective that indicates possession before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
options.B: An adjective that points out a noun
options.C: An adjective that introduces a question before a noun
options.D: An adjective that refers to members of a group individually

questions.explanation: A possessive adjective or determiner indicates possession before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. Example: 'Their house is large.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an interrogative adjective or determiner?

options.A: An adjective that introduces a question before a noun: which book, what time, whose bag
options.B: An adjective that points out a noun
options.D: An adjective that refers to members of a group individually

questions.explanation: An interrogative adjective or determiner introduces a question before a noun: which book, what time, whose bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a distributive adjective or determiner?

options.A: An adjective that refers to members of a group individually: each student, every child, either road, neither answer
options.B: An adjective that points out a noun
options.D: An adjective that introduces a question

questions.explanation: A distributive adjective or determiner refers to members of a group individually: each student, every child, either road, neither answer.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adjective of origin or proper adjective?

options.A: An adjective derived from a proper noun that usually begins with a capital letter
options.B: An adjective that indicates an amount of an uncountable noun
options.C: An adjective that indicates number or order
options.D: An adjective that points out a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective of origin or proper adjective is derived from a proper noun and usually begins with a capital letter. Examples: Indian culture, Shakespearean drama, Victorian architecture.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the three degrees of comparison?

options.A: Positive, comparative and superlative

questions.explanation: The three degrees of comparison are positive, comparative and superlative.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the positive degree?

options.A: It expresses a quality without comparison
options.B: It compares two people or things
options.C: It expresses the highest or lowest degree within a group of three or more

questions.explanation: The positive degree expresses a quality without comparison. Example: 'Ravi is tall.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the comparative degree?

options.A: It compares two people or things
options.B: It expresses a quality without comparison
options.C: It expresses the highest or lowest degree within a group of three or more

questions.explanation: The comparative degree compares two people or things. It is commonly formed with -er or more. Example: 'Ravi is taller than Mohan.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the superlative degree?

options.A: It expresses the highest or lowest degree within a group of three or more
options.B: It compares two people or things
options.C: It expresses a quality without comparison

questions.explanation: The superlative degree expresses the highest or lowest degree within a group of three or more. It is commonly formed with -est or most. Example: 'Ravi is the tallest boy in the class.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are many short adjectives compared?

options.A: Add -er for the comparative and -est for the superlative
options.C: Change y to i and add -er/-est
options.D: Double the final consonant and add -ed

questions.explanation: Many short adjectives add -er for the comparative and -est for the superlative: small-smaller-smallest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are adjectives ending in consonant + y compared?

options.A: Change y to i and add -er/-est

questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in consonant + y change y to i and add -er/-est: happy-happier-happiest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to a final consonant after a short stressed vowel?

options.A: It is often doubled before -er/-est

questions.explanation: A final consonant after a short stressed vowel is often doubled before -er/-est: big-bigger-biggest; hot-hotter-hottest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are many longer adjectives compared?

options.A: Use more and most
options.C: Change y to i and add -er/-est

questions.explanation: Many longer adjectives use more and most: beautiful-more beautiful-most beautiful.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'good'?

options.A: gooder, goodest

questions.explanation: Good has irregular comparison: good-better-best.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'bad'?

options.A: badder, baddest

questions.explanation: Bad has irregular comparison: bad-worse-worst.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'far'?

options.A: farer, farest

questions.explanation: Far has irregular comparison: far-farther/further-farthest/furthest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'little'?

options.A: littler, littlest

questions.explanation: Little has irregular comparison: little-less-least.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the comparative and superlative forms of 'many/much'?

options.A: manyer, manyest

questions.explanation: Many/much have irregular comparison: many/much-more-most.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'farther' and 'further'?

options.A: Farther is commonly used for physical distance; further commonly means additional or more
options.B: Farther means additional; further means physical distance
options.C: Both mean the same in all contexts
options.D: Farther is used only with uncountable nouns

questions.explanation: Farther is commonly used for physical distance; further commonly means additional or more, though usage overlaps.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct pattern for comparing two things?

options.A: Use the comparative degree, not the superlative
options.D: Use both comparative and superlative together

questions.explanation: Use the comparative degree, not the superlative: 'Of the two plans, this one is better.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct use of 'as...as'?

options.A: Use the positive degree between as and as
options.B: Use the comparative degree between as and as
options.C: Use the superlative degree between as and as

questions.explanation: Use the positive degree between as and as: 'She is as tall as her sister.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the correct use of 'not so/as...as'?

options.A: It expresses inequality using the positive degree
options.B: It expresses inequality using the comparative degree
options.C: It expresses equality using the superlative degree
options.D: It expresses inequality using the superlative degree

questions.explanation: Not so/as...as expresses inequality using the positive degree: 'This road is not as wide as that road.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'more better' generally incorrect?

options.A: Because better is already the comparative form of good; do not add more to it in standard usage
options.D: Because better is a positive degree

questions.explanation: Better is already the comparative form of good; do not add more to it in standard usage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why is 'most tallest' incorrect?

options.A: Because tallest is already the superlative form; use either tallest or most tall, not both together
options.B: Because tallest is a comparative form
options.C: Because most is a comparative form
options.D: Because tallest is a positive degree

questions.explanation: Tallest is already the superlative form; use either tallest or, where appropriate, most tall, not both together.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the usual order of adjectives before a noun?

options.A: Opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose, then the noun
options.B: Colour, size, opinion, age, shape, material, origin, purpose
options.C: Material, purpose, origin, colour, shape, age, size, opinion
options.D: Size, opinion, colour, age, origin, shape, purpose, material

questions.explanation: A common order is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose and then the noun. Example: 'a beautiful small old round brown Italian wooden dining table.' The order is a tendency, not an inflexible rule.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are coordinate adjectives?

options.A: Adjectives that independently modify the same noun and can often be joined by 'and' or separated by commas
options.B: Adjectives that build meaning in a fixed order and are not normally separated by commas
options.C: Adjectives that follow the noun they modify
options.D: Adjectives that appear after a linking verb

questions.explanation: Coordinate adjectives independently modify the same noun and can often be joined by and or separated by commas. Example: 'a long, difficult examination.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are cumulative adjectives?

options.A: Adjectives that build meaning in a fixed order and are not normally separated by commas
options.B: Adjectives that independently modify the same noun and can be joined by 'and'
options.C: Adjectives that follow the noun they modify
options.D: Adjectives that appear after a linking verb

questions.explanation: Cumulative adjectives build meaning in a fixed order and are not normally separated by commas. Example: 'three large wooden boxes.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb?

options.A: A word that modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or sometimes an entire clause
options.B: A word that modifies a noun
options.C: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: An adverb modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or sometimes an entire clause. It commonly gives information about manner, place, time, frequency, degree or viewpoint.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which questions can an adverb answer?

options.A: How? Where? When? How often? To what extent? and sometimes Why?
options.B: What kind? Which one? How many? How much?

questions.explanation: An adverb can answer How? Where? When? How often? To what extent? and sometimes Why?

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of manner?

options.A: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.B: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.C: An adverb that tells when an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells how often an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of manner tells how an action is performed. Examples: slowly, carefully, well, politely. Sentence: 'She spoke politely.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of place?

options.A: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells when an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells how often an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of place tells where an action occurs. Examples: here, there, outside, nearby, everywhere.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of time?

options.A: An adverb that tells when an action occurs
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells how often an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of time tells when an action occurs. Examples: now, yesterday, soon, later, already.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of frequency?

options.A: An adverb that tells how often an action occurs
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells when an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency tells how often an action occurs. Examples: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of degree?

options.A: An adverb that tells the intensity or extent of an action, adjective or adverb
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells how often an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of degree tells the intensity or extent of an action, adjective or adverb. Examples: very, too, quite, almost, extremely, enough.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an adverb of affirmation or negation?

options.A: An adverb that expresses confirmation or denial
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that tells when an action occurs

questions.explanation: An adverb of affirmation or negation expresses confirmation or denial. Examples: certainly, surely, definitely, not, never.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a sentence adverb?

options.A: An adverb that comments on the whole sentence or the speaker's attitude
options.B: An adverb that tells how an action is performed
options.C: An adverb that tells where an action occurs
options.D: An adverb that modifies a noun

questions.explanation: A sentence adverb comments on the whole sentence or the speaker's attitude. Examples: 'Fortunately, the train arrived on time'; 'Honestly, I disagree.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an interrogative adverb?

options.A: An adverb that asks a question about time, place, manner or reason: when, where, how, why
options.B: An adverb that introduces a clause and relates it to a time, place or reason
options.C: An adverb that comments on the whole sentence
options.D: An adverb that tells the intensity of an action

questions.explanation: An interrogative adverb asks a question about time, place, manner or reason: when, where, how, why.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a relative adverb?

options.A: An adverb that introduces a clause and relates it to a time, place or reason: when, where, why
options.B: An adverb that asks a question
options.C: An adverb that comments on the whole sentence
options.D: An adverb that tells the intensity of an action

questions.explanation: A relative adverb introduces a clause and relates it to a time, place or reason: when, where, why. Example: 'I remember the day when we met.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are many adverbs of manner formed?

options.A: By adding -ly to an adjective

questions.explanation: Many adverbs of manner are formed by adding -ly to an adjective: quick-quickly, careful-carefully. Not all adverbs end in -ly.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following common adverbs does NOT end in -ly?

options.A: quickly

questions.explanation: Common adverbs that do not end in -ly include fast, hard, late, early, well, straight.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'hard' and 'hardly'?

options.A: Hard means with effort or intensity; hardly means almost not
options.B: Hard means almost not; hardly means with effort

questions.explanation: Hard means with effort or intensity; hardly means almost not. 'He works hard' differs from 'He hardly works.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'late' and 'lately'?

options.A: Late means after the expected time; lately means recently
options.B: Late means recently; lately means after the expected time
options.D: Both mean after the expected time

questions.explanation: Late means after the expected time; lately means recently.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'high' and 'highly'?

options.A: High often refers to physical height or level; highly often means very or to a great degree
options.B: High means very; highly means physical height

questions.explanation: High often refers to physical height or level; highly often means very or to a great degree. Example: 'The bird flew high'; 'She is highly respected.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'near' and 'nearly'?

options.A: Near means close; nearly means almost
options.B: Near means almost; nearly means close

questions.explanation: Near means close; nearly means almost.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where does an adverb of frequency usually appear with an ordinary main verb?

options.A: Before the main verb

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency usually appears before an ordinary main verb: 'She often visits us.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where does an adverb of frequency usually appear with the verb 'be'?

options.A: After the finite form of 'be'

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency usually appears after the finite form of be: 'She is always punctual.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where does an adverb of frequency usually appear with an auxiliary verb?

options.A: After the first auxiliary

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency generally appears after the first auxiliary: 'They have never visited Delhi'; 'I can usually help.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where does 'enough' appear when it modifies an adjective or adverb?

options.A: It normally follows the adjective or adverb
options.B: It normally comes before the adjective or adverb
options.D: It normally comes before the subject

questions.explanation: Enough normally follows the adjective or adverb: old enough; quickly enough.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Where does 'enough' appear when it modifies a noun?

options.A: It normally comes before the noun
options.D: It normally comes after the verb

questions.explanation: Enough normally comes before the noun: enough time; enough money.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'too' and 'very'?

options.A: Very indicates a high degree; too usually means more than is desirable or acceptable
options.B: Very means more than desirable; too indicates a high degree
options.D: Too indicates a low degree; very indicates excess

questions.explanation: Very indicates a high degree; too usually means more than is desirable or acceptable. 'Very difficult' does not necessarily mean impossible; 'too difficult' suggests excessive difficulty.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'so' and 'such'?

options.A: So usually modifies an adjective or adverb; such modifies a noun phrase
options.B: So modifies a noun phrase; such modifies an adjective

questions.explanation: So usually modifies an adjective or adverb (so beautiful); such modifies a noun phrase (such a beautiful place).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'sometime', 'sometimes' and 'some time'?

options.A: Sometime means at an unspecified time; sometimes means occasionally; some time means a period of time
options.B: Sometime means occasionally; sometimes means at an unspecified time; some time means a period of time
options.D: Sometimes means a period of time; some time means occasionally

questions.explanation: Sometime means at an unspecified time; sometimes means occasionally; some time means a period of time.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'every day' and 'everyday'?

options.A: Every day means each day; everyday is an adjective meaning ordinary or usual
options.B: Every day is an adjective; everyday means each day

questions.explanation: Every day means each day; everyday is an adjective meaning ordinary or usual. Example: 'I exercise every day'; 'These are everyday clothes.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can an adverb modify an adjective?

options.A: Yes, for example 'The question is extremely difficult.'

questions.explanation: An adverb can modify an adjective: 'The question is extremely difficult.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can an adverb modify another adverb?

options.A: Yes, for example 'She runs very quickly.'
options.D: Yes, but only in negative sentences

questions.explanation: An adverb can modify another adverb: 'She runs very quickly.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a preposition?

options.A: A word or multi-word unit that expresses a relationship between a noun phrase or pronoun and another part of the sentence
options.B: A word that modifies a verb
options.D: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: A preposition expresses a relationship between a noun phrase or pronoun and another part of the sentence. It can indicate place, time, direction, cause, means, possession or other relationships.

questions.subject: English
