questions.question: What is a prepositional phrase?

options.A: A preposition and its complement, usually a noun phrase or pronoun
options.B: A group of words containing a subject and a finite verb
options.C: A word that modifies a verb
options.D: A group of adjectives before a noun

questions.explanation: A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition and its complement, usually a noun phrase or pronoun. Example: under the table, after lunch, with her.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a preposition of place?

options.A: A preposition that indicates location or position
options.B: A preposition that indicates when something happens
options.C: A preposition that indicates movement or direction
options.D: A preposition that indicates the agent in a passive sentence

questions.explanation: A preposition of place indicates location or position. Examples: in, on, at, under, above, below, beside, between, among, behind, in front of.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a preposition of time?

options.A: A preposition that indicates when something happens
options.B: A preposition that indicates location or position
options.C: A preposition that indicates movement or direction
options.D: A preposition that indicates the instrument used

questions.explanation: A preposition of time indicates when something happens. Examples: at, on, in, since, for, during, by, until, before, after.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a preposition of direction or movement?

options.A: A preposition that indicates movement or direction
options.B: A preposition that indicates location or position
options.C: A preposition that indicates when something happens
options.D: A preposition that indicates the agent in a passive sentence

questions.explanation: A preposition of direction or movement indicates movement or direction. Examples: to, towards, into, onto, through, across, along, from, out of.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a preposition of agent or instrument?

options.A: By commonly indicates the agent in a passive sentence; with commonly indicates an instrument
options.B: By indicates an instrument; with indicates the agent

questions.explanation: By commonly indicates the agent in a passive sentence; with commonly indicates an instrument. Example: 'The letter was written by Ravi'; 'She cut it with a knife.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a simple preposition?

options.A: A preposition consisting of one word, such as in, on, at, by, for, from, with
options.B: A preposition formed from more than one element
options.C: A group of words functioning as a preposition
options.D: A preposition followed by a clause

questions.explanation: A simple preposition consists of one word, such as in, on, at, by, for, from, with.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a compound preposition?

options.A: A preposition formed from more than one element or a prefixed form, such as inside, outside, within, without, into, upon
options.B: A preposition consisting of one word
options.C: A group of words functioning as a preposition
options.D: A preposition followed by a clause

questions.explanation: A compound preposition is formed from more than one element or a prefixed form, such as inside, outside, within, without, into, upon.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a phrase preposition?

options.A: A group of words functioning as a preposition
options.B: A preposition consisting of one word
options.C: A preposition formed from a prefixed form
options.D: A preposition followed by a clause

questions.explanation: A phrase preposition is a group of words functioning as a preposition. Examples: because of, in front of, in spite of, according to, on behalf of, with regard to.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'at' used for time?

options.A: For precise clock times and certain fixed expressions
options.C: With months, years, seasons and centuries

questions.explanation: At is used for precise clock times and certain fixed expressions: at 6 p.m., at noon, at midnight, at night.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'on' used for time?

options.A: With days and dates

questions.explanation: On is used with days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August, on my birthday.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'in' used for time?

options.A: With months, years, seasons, centuries and longer periods

questions.explanation: In is used with months, years, seasons, centuries and longer periods: in July, in 2026, in winter, in the 21st century.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'at' used for place?

options.A: It commonly indicates a point or specific location
options.B: It indicates being inside an enclosed space
options.C: It indicates a surface or position along a line
options.D: It indicates movement from outside to inside

questions.explanation: At commonly indicates a point or specific location: at the bus stop, at the entrance, at school.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'in' used for place?

options.A: It indicates being inside an enclosed space or within an area
options.B: It indicates a point or specific location
options.C: It indicates a surface or position along a line
options.D: It indicates movement to a surface

questions.explanation: In indicates being inside an enclosed space or within an area: in the room, in Bengaluru, in India.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'on' used for place?

options.A: It indicates a surface or position along a line or route
options.B: It indicates being inside an enclosed space
options.C: It indicates a point or specific location
options.D: It indicates movement from outside to inside

questions.explanation: On indicates a surface or position along a line or route: on the table, on the wall, on the road.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'since' and 'for'?

options.A: Since gives the starting point of a period; for gives its duration
options.B: Since gives duration; for gives the starting point

questions.explanation: Since gives the starting point of a period; for gives its duration. Example: 'since Monday'; 'for three days.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'by' and 'until'?

options.A: By means not later than a deadline; until means continuing up to a point
options.B: By means continuing up to a point; until means not later than a deadline
options.C: Both mean not later than a deadline
options.D: Both mean continuing up to a point

questions.explanation: By means not later than a deadline; until means continuing up to a point. 'Submit it by Friday' differs from 'Stay here until Friday.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'between' and 'among'?

options.A: Between is traditionally used for distinct, individually considered items (including more than two); among is used for a group or mass
options.B: Between is used for groups; among is used for two items only
options.C: Both are used only for two items
options.D: Both are used only for groups

questions.explanation: Between is traditionally used for distinct, individually considered items (including more than two); among is used for a group or mass. Example: 'between the three candidates'; 'among the crowd.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'beside' and 'besides'?

options.A: Beside means next to; besides means in addition to or apart from
options.B: Beside means in addition to; besides means next to

questions.explanation: Beside means next to; besides means in addition to or apart from.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'in' and 'into'?

options.A: In commonly indicates position; into indicates movement from outside to inside
options.B: In indicates movement; into indicates position

questions.explanation: In commonly indicates position; into indicates movement from outside to inside. Example: 'The child is in the room'; 'The child ran into the room.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'on' and 'onto'?

options.A: On commonly indicates position; onto indicates movement to a surface
options.B: On indicates movement; onto indicates position

questions.explanation: On commonly indicates position; onto indicates movement to a surface. Example: 'The book is on the desk'; 'Put the book onto the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'above' and 'over'?

options.A: Over often suggests covering, movement across or directly higher; above generally indicates a higher level or position
options.B: Above suggests covering; over indicates a higher level only

questions.explanation: Both can indicate a higher position. Over often suggests covering, movement across or directly higher; above generally indicates a higher level or position.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'below' and 'under'?

options.A: Under often suggests directly beneath or covered by; below often indicates a lower level or rank
options.B: Below suggests directly beneath; under indicates a lower level only

questions.explanation: Both indicate a lower position. Under often suggests directly beneath or covered by; below often indicates a lower level or rank.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'good' when referring to skill?

options.A: good at

questions.explanation: Good at is used for skill: 'She is good at mathematics.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'interested'?

options.A: interested in

questions.explanation: Interested in: 'He is interested in science.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'depend'?

options.A: depend on/upon

questions.explanation: Depend on/upon: 'Success depends on effort.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'prefer'?

options.A: prefer X to Y

questions.explanation: Prefer X to Y: 'I prefer tea to coffee.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'married'?

options.A: married to

questions.explanation: Married to: 'She is married to a doctor.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'afraid'?

options.A: afraid of

questions.explanation: Afraid of: 'The child is afraid of dogs.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'consist'?

options.A: consist of

questions.explanation: Consist of: 'The team consists of eleven players.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'belong'?

options.A: belong to

questions.explanation: Belong to: 'This book belongs to me.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'arrive'?

options.A: arrive at for many specific places and arrive in for cities or countries

questions.explanation: Use arrive at for many specific places and arrive in for cities or countries: 'arrive at the station'; 'arrive in Bengaluru.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'listen'?

options.A: listen to

questions.explanation: Listen to: 'Listen to the teacher.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'wait'?

options.A: wait for

questions.explanation: Wait for: 'Wait for the bus.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'congratulate'?

options.A: congratulate someone on an achievement

questions.explanation: Congratulate someone on an achievement: 'They congratulated her on her success.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'accuse'?

options.A: accuse someone of something

questions.explanation: Accuse someone of something: 'He was accused of theft.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which preposition follows 'prevent'?

options.A: prevent someone from doing something

questions.explanation: Prevent someone from doing something: 'The rain prevented us from playing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for a preposition followed by a pronoun?

options.A: Use the object form: for me, with him, between us, to them
options.B: Use the subject form: for I, with he, between we, to they

questions.explanation: Use the object form after a preposition: for me, with him, between us, to them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a sentence end with a preposition?

options.A: Yes, ending a sentence with a preposition is grammatical in many natural English constructions, especially questions and relative clauses
options.B: No, a sentence can never end with a preposition
options.C: Yes, but only in formal writing
options.D: No, prepositions must always come first

questions.explanation: Ending a sentence with a preposition is grammatical in many natural English constructions, especially questions and relative clauses: 'Who are you talking to?' Formal alternatives are possible but should not be forced.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a conjunction?

options.A: A word or expression that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences
options.B: A word that modifies a verb
options.C: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: A conjunction is a word or expression that connects words, phrases, clauses or sentences.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: A conjunction that connects grammatical units of equal rank
options.B: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause
options.C: A conjunction that works in pairs
options.D: A conjunction that connects only sentences

questions.explanation: A coordinating conjunction connects grammatical units of equal rank, such as two words, phrases or independent clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the seven common coordinating conjunctions?

options.A: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
options.B: because, although, if, unless, when, while, since
options.C: either, neither, both, not only, whether, rather, than
options.D: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise, furthermore

questions.explanation: The seven common coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so, often remembered by the acronym FANBOYS.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'and' express?

options.A: It adds or combines information

questions.explanation: And adds or combines information: 'Ravi and Rani attended the meeting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'but' express?

options.A: It expresses contrast

questions.explanation: But expresses contrast: 'He is poor but honest.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'or' express?

options.A: It presents alternatives

questions.explanation: Or presents alternatives: 'Would you like tea or coffee?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'nor' express?

options.A: It adds a negative alternative and commonly follows a negative statement or neither

questions.explanation: Nor adds a negative alternative and commonly follows a negative statement or neither: 'He did not call, nor did he write.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'yet' express?

options.A: It expresses contrast or an unexpected result

questions.explanation: Yet expresses contrast or an unexpected result: 'The task was difficult, yet she completed it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does the coordinating conjunction 'so' express?

options.A: It can express a result

questions.explanation: So can express a result: 'It was raining, so we stayed indoors.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'for' express as a conjunction?

options.A: It can introduce a reason in a formal or literary style

questions.explanation: For can introduce a reason in a formal or literary style: 'I stayed indoors, for it was raining.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause and shows its relationship to an independent clause
options.B: A conjunction that connects units of equal rank
options.C: A conjunction that works in pairs
options.D: A conjunction that connects only words

questions.explanation: A subordinating conjunction introduces a dependent clause and shows its relationship to an independent clause. Examples: because, although, though, if, unless, when, while, before, after, since, until, as, whereas.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a subordinating conjunction?

options.A: and

questions.explanation: Although is a subordinating conjunction that introduces a dependent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a correlative conjunction?

options.A: Conjunctions that work in pairs to connect balanced grammatical elements
options.B: Conjunctions that connect units of equal rank singly
options.D: Adverbs that connect ideas between clauses

questions.explanation: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs to connect balanced grammatical elements. Examples: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or, rather...than.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a pair of correlative conjunctions?

options.A: and...but

questions.explanation: Either...or is a pair of correlative conjunctions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the rule for either...or and neither...nor agreement?

options.A: When they join two subjects, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject
options.B: The verb always takes the plural form
options.C: The verb always takes the singular form
options.D: The verb agrees with the first subject only

questions.explanation: When they join two subjects, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: 'Either the manager or the workers are coming'; 'Either the workers or the manager is coming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is parallelism with correlative conjunctions?

options.A: The grammatical forms after both parts of the pair should be balanced
options.B: The first part must be a noun and the second a verb
options.C: Only the second part needs to be grammatically correct
options.D: The pair must always be followed by a clause

questions.explanation: The grammatical forms after both parts of the pair should be balanced. Correct: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking'; 'He likes both reading and writing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a conjunctive adverb?

options.A: An adverb that connects ideas between clauses or sentences and expresses a logical relationship
options.B: A conjunction that connects units of equal rank
options.C: A conjunction that introduces a dependent clause
options.D: A conjunction that works in pairs

questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb connects ideas between clauses or sentences and expresses a logical relationship. Examples: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise, furthermore. It is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is punctuation commonly used with a conjunctive adverb joining independent clauses?

options.A: Use a semicolon before it and a comma after it
options.B: Use a comma before it and a semicolon after it
options.D: Use a colon before it and a full stop after it

questions.explanation: Use a semicolon before it and a comma after it: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took another route.' A full stop can also separate the clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'although' and 'despite'?

options.A: Although is a conjunction followed by a clause; despite is a preposition followed by a noun phrase or gerund
options.B: Although is a preposition; despite is a conjunction
options.C: Both are followed by a clause
options.D: Both are followed by a noun phrase only

questions.explanation: Although is a conjunction followed by a clause; despite is a preposition followed by a noun phrase or gerund. Examples: 'Although it rained, we played'; 'Despite the rain, we played.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'because' and 'because of'?

options.A: Because is a conjunction followed by a clause; because of is a prepositional expression followed by a noun phrase or gerund
options.B: Because is a preposition; because of is a conjunction
options.C: Both are followed by a clause
options.D: Both are followed by a noun phrase only

questions.explanation: Because is a conjunction followed by a clause; because of is a prepositional expression followed by a noun phrase or gerund.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'unless' and 'if...not'?

options.A: Unless means 'except if' or 'if not'; avoid adding another negative when it creates an unintended double negative
options.D: Unless is followed by a noun phrase; if...not by a clause

questions.explanation: Unless means 'except if' or 'if not'. Avoid adding another negative when it creates an unintended double negative. Example: 'Unless you study, you may fail.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'so...that' and 'such...that'?

options.A: So is followed by an adjective/adverb and that clause; such is followed by a noun phrase and that clause
options.B: So is followed by a noun phrase; such is followed by an adjective
options.C: Both are followed by a noun phrase
options.D: Both are followed by an adjective only

questions.explanation: So is followed by an adjective/adverb and that clause ('so tired that he slept'); such is followed by a noun phrase and that clause ('such a difficult task that we needed help').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'while' and 'whereas'?

options.A: Both can show contrast; while can also indicate simultaneous time; whereas is used mainly to contrast two facts
options.B: While is used only for time; whereas is used only for time
options.C: Both are used only for simultaneous time
options.D: Whereas can indicate simultaneous time; while cannot

questions.explanation: Both can show contrast; while can also indicate simultaneous time. Whereas is used mainly to contrast two facts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'as' and 'because'?

options.A: Both can introduce reasons; because normally gives a more direct or prominent reason; as often introduces a reason treated as background information
options.B: As gives a more direct reason; because introduces background information
options.C: Both are used only for comparison
options.D: As is used only for time; because is used only for contrast

questions.explanation: Both can introduce reasons. Because normally gives a more direct or prominent reason; as often introduces a reason treated as background information.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a clause?

options.A: A group of words containing a subject and a verb
options.B: A group of words without a verb
options.D: A group of adjectives before a noun

questions.explanation: A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a simple sentence?

options.A: A sentence that contains one independent clause
options.B: A sentence that contains two independent clauses
options.C: A sentence that contains one independent and one dependent clause

questions.explanation: A simple sentence contains one independent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a compound sentence?

options.A: A sentence that contains two or more independent clauses, commonly joined by a coordinating conjunction or separated by a semicolon
options.B: A sentence that contains one independent clause
options.C: A sentence that contains one independent and one dependent clause

questions.explanation: A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses, commonly joined by a coordinating conjunction or separated by a semicolon.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a complex sentence?

options.A: A sentence that contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause
options.B: A sentence that contains only one independent clause
options.C: A sentence that contains two independent clauses

questions.explanation: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an interjection?

options.A: A word or short expression that conveys a sudden feeling, reaction or emotion and is often grammatically independent of the rest of the sentence
options.C: A word that modifies a verb
options.D: A word that replaces a noun

questions.explanation: An interjection is a word or short expression that conveys a sudden feeling, reaction or emotion and is often grammatically independent of the rest of the sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are common interjections of sorrow or disappointment?

options.A: Hurrah! Hurray!

questions.explanation: Common interjections of sorrow or disappointment include Alas! Oh no!

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are common interjections of surprise?

options.A: Oh! Ah! What! Wow!

questions.explanation: Common interjections of surprise include Oh! Ah! What! Wow!

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are common interjections used to attract attention?

options.A: Hurrah! Wow!

questions.explanation: Common interjections used to attract attention include Hey! Look! Listen!

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are common interjections of approval or appreciation?

options.A: Alas! Oh no!

questions.explanation: Common interjections of approval or appreciation include Bravo! Well done! Excellent!

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following are common interjections of pain?

options.A: Hurrah! Wow!

questions.explanation: Common interjections of pain include Ouch! Ah!

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What punctuation mark commonly follows a strong interjection?

options.A: An exclamation mark

questions.explanation: An exclamation mark is commonly used: 'Alas! We lost the match.' A comma may be used for a milder interruption: 'Well, let us begin.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does an interjection normally have a grammatical connection to the sentence?

options.A: No, it generally expresses emotion independently
options.B: Yes, it is always the subject of the sentence
options.C: Yes, it is always the verb of the sentence
options.D: Yes, it always agrees with the subject

questions.explanation: An interjection generally expresses emotion independently: 'Oh, I forgot my keys.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between an interjection and an exclamatory sentence?

options.A: An interjection is a word or short expression of feeling; an exclamatory sentence is a complete sentence expressing strong emotion
options.B: An interjection is a complete sentence; an exclamatory sentence is a single word

questions.explanation: An interjection is a word or short expression of feeling; an exclamatory sentence is a complete sentence expressing strong emotion. 'Wow!' is an interjection; 'What a beautiful day it is!' is an exclamatory sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are articles?

options.A: Determiners used before nouns to indicate whether the noun refers to something specific or non-specific

questions.explanation: Articles are determiners used before nouns to indicate whether the noun refers to something specific or non-specific. English has three articles: a, an and the.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the two main types of articles?

options.A: A and an are indefinite articles; the is the definite article
options.B: A and the are indefinite articles; an is the definite article
options.C: The and an are indefinite articles; a is the definite article

questions.explanation: A and an are indefinite articles; the is the definite article.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'a' used?

options.A: Before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound, when the noun is not specifically identified
options.B: Before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound

questions.explanation: A is used before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound, when the noun is not specifically identified. Examples: a book, a university, a European country.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'an' used?

options.A: Before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound
options.B: Before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound

questions.explanation: An is used before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound. Examples: an apple, an hour, an honest man, an MBA graduate.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is the choice between 'a' and 'an' based on spelling or sound?

options.A: It is based on pronunciation, not merely the first written letter
options.B: It is based only on the first written letter
options.C: It is based on the last letter of the word
options.D: It is based on the number of syllables

questions.explanation: It is based on pronunciation, not merely the first written letter. Use a university because it begins with the /ju/ consonant sound; use an hour because the h is silent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used?

options.A: When the listener or reader can identify the particular person or thing, when it has already been mentioned, when it is unique in the context, or when the noun is made specific by a phrase or clause

questions.explanation: The is used when the listener or reader can identify the particular person or thing, when it has already been mentioned, when it is unique in the context, or when the noun is made specific by a phrase or clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the first-mention and second-mention rule?

options.A: A singular countable noun is often introduced with a/an and referred to later with the
options.B: A singular countable noun is introduced with the and referred to later with a/an

questions.explanation: A singular countable noun is often introduced with a/an and referred to later with the: 'I saw a dog. The dog was black.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used with unique things?

options.A: With entities understood as unique in the context: the Sun, the Moon, the Earth, the sky

questions.explanation: Use the with entities understood as unique in the context: the Sun, the Moon, the Earth, the sky. Capitalisation conventions for astronomical names may vary.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used with superlative adjectives?

options.A: Before a superlative adjective in ordinary attributive use

questions.explanation: Use the before a superlative adjective in ordinary attributive use: the tallest building, the most useful book.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used with ordinal numbers?

options.A: In expressions such as the first chapter, the second question, the last day

questions.explanation: Use the in expressions such as the first chapter, the second question, the last day.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used with rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges?

options.A: With names such as the Ganga, the Nile, the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas

questions.explanation: Use the with names such as the Ganga, the Nile, the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' used with plural names of countries or political/geographical units?

options.A: With names such as the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and with many names containing terms such as Republic or Kingdom

questions.explanation: Use the with names such as the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and with many names containing terms such as Republic or Kingdom.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is 'the' used before the names of most countries, cities and continents?

options.A: No; usually say India, Japan, Karnataka, Bengaluru, Asia, not the India or the Bengaluru
options.B: Yes, always use the before all country names
options.C: Yes, always use the before all city names
options.D: Yes, always use the before all continent names

questions.explanation: Usually say India, Japan, Karnataka, Bengaluru, Asia, not the India or the Bengaluru.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' omitted before languages and school subjects?

options.A: Articles are normally omitted when referring to languages and academic subjects generally
options.B: The is always used before languages
options.C: The is always used before academic subjects
options.D: A is always used before languages

questions.explanation: Articles are normally omitted when referring to languages and academic subjects generally: Kannada, English, mathematics, history.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' omitted before meals?

options.A: Articles are commonly omitted when meals are referred to generally
options.B: The is always used before meals
options.C: A is always used before meals
options.D: An is always used before meals

questions.explanation: Articles are commonly omitted when meals are referred to generally: 'We have breakfast at eight.' An article may be used when the meal is specified or described: 'The breakfast served at the hotel was excellent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is 'the' omitted before plural and uncountable nouns used generally?

options.A: Use no article for general reference; use the when referring to a specific group or amount
options.B: Always use the before plural nouns
options.C: Always use the before uncountable nouns
options.D: Always use a before plural nouns

questions.explanation: Use no article for general reference: 'Books are useful'; 'Water is essential.' Use the when referring to a specific group or amount: 'The books on this shelf are mine'; 'The water in this bottle is cold.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the zero article?

options.A: It means that no article is used before a noun; it commonly occurs with plural and uncountable nouns in general statements, most proper names, languages, subjects and certain fixed expressions
options.B: It means using 'a' before a noun
options.C: It means using 'the' before a noun
options.D: It means using 'an' before a noun

questions.explanation: The zero article means that no article is used before a noun. It commonly occurs with plural and uncountable nouns in general statements, most proper names, languages, subjects and certain fixed expressions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is an article omitted before a person's name?

options.A: Articles are normally omitted before personal names
options.B: The is always used before personal names
options.C: A is always used before personal names
options.D: An is always used before personal names

questions.explanation: Articles are normally omitted before personal names: Ravi is here, not ordinarily the Ravi is here.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is an article used with a profession?

options.A: Use a/an before a singular countable profession
options.B: Use the before a singular countable profession
options.C: Use no article before a profession

questions.explanation: Use a/an before a singular countable profession: 'She is a doctor'; 'He is an engineer.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What article is used with a singular countable noun when it is mentioned generally?

options.A: A singular countable noun generally needs a determiner: 'A tiger is a wild animal' or 'The tiger is a wild animal'

questions.explanation: A singular countable noun generally needs a determiner: 'A tiger is a wild animal' or 'The tiger is a wild animal.' Bare singular countable nouns are normally not used in this way.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What article is used with musical instruments?

options.A: In the traditional pattern for ability or performance, use 'the'

questions.explanation: In the traditional pattern for ability or performance, use the: 'She plays the violin.' Modern usage can vary in some contexts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What article is used with newspapers?

options.A: Use 'the' with newspaper titles when the title convention includes it, for example The Hindu and The Times of India
options.D: Use no article with newspaper titles

questions.explanation: Use the with newspaper titles when the title convention includes it, for example The Hindu and The Times of India.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What article is used with inventions when referring to a whole class?

options.A: Both the definite article and a plural generic form are possible

questions.explanation: Both the definite article and a plural generic form are possible: 'The telephone changed communication' or 'Telephones changed communication.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'a few' and 'few'?

options.A: A few means some; few means almost none; both are used with plural countable nouns
options.B: A few means almost none; few means some
options.D: Both are used with uncountable nouns

questions.explanation: A few means some; few means almost none. Both are used with plural countable nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'a little' and 'little'?

options.A: A little means some; little means almost none; both are used with uncountable nouns
options.B: A little means almost none; little means some
options.D: Both are used with countable nouns

questions.explanation: A little means some; little means almost none. Both are used with uncountable nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'a number of' and 'the number of'?

options.A: A number of means several and takes a plural verb; the number of refers to the total and takes a singular verb
options.B: A number of takes a singular verb; the number of takes a plural verb

questions.explanation: A number of means several and takes a plural verb: 'A number of students are absent.' The number of refers to the total and takes a singular verb: 'The number of students is increasing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'a Mr Sharma' and 'Mr Sharma'?

options.A: Mr Sharma identifies a person by title and name; a Mr Sharma can mean a person called Mr Sharma who is not known to the speaker or is being introduced as one among others
options.B: A Mr Sharma identifies a known person; Mr Sharma means an unknown person
options.D: A Mr Sharma is always incorrect

questions.explanation: Mr Sharma identifies a person by title and name. A Mr Sharma can mean a person called Mr Sharma who is not known to the speaker or is being introduced as one among others.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the article rule with abbreviations?

options.A: Choose a/an according to the initial spoken sound, not the written letter
options.B: Choose a/an according to the first written letter only

questions.explanation: Choose a/an according to the initial spoken sound, not the written letter. Examples: an FIR (said 'ef...'), an MLA, a UNESCO body (if pronounced with /ju/), an X-ray.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'in hospital' and 'in the hospital'?

options.A: In British English, in hospital can mean being a patient; in the hospital identifies the building or is common in American English
options.B: In hospital identifies the building; in the hospital means being a patient

questions.explanation: In British English, in hospital can mean being a patient; in the hospital identifies the building or is common in American English. Context and variety of English matter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'go to school' and 'go to the school'?

options.A: Go to school commonly means attend school as a student; go to the school refers to going to a particular school building or institution for a specific purpose
options.B: Go to school refers to the building; go to the school means attend as a student
options.C: Both mean attend school as a student
options.D: Both refer to the building only

questions.explanation: Go to school commonly means attend school as a student; go to the school refers to going to a particular school building or institution for a specific purpose.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: Can one English word belong to more than one part of speech?

options.A: Yes, its grammatical category depends on its use in the sentence
options.B: No, every word has only one fixed part of speech
options.C: Only nouns can belong to more than one part of speech
options.D: Only verbs can belong to more than one part of speech

questions.explanation: Yes. Its grammatical category depends on its use in the sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'The bag is light'?

options.A: Adjective

questions.explanation: It is an adjective because it describes the bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'Please light the lamp'?

options.A: Verb

questions.explanation: It is a verb because it expresses an action.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'Turn on the light'?

options.A: Noun

questions.explanation: It is a noun because it names a thing.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'fast' in 'He drives fast'?

options.A: Adverb

questions.explanation: It is an adverb because it modifies the verb drives.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'fast' in 'He is a fast runner'?

options.A: Adjective

questions.explanation: It is an adjective because it modifies the noun runner.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'before' in 'I have seen him before'?

options.A: Adverb

questions.explanation: It is an adverb because it modifies the verb phrase and has no noun phrase complement.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'before' in 'Come before lunch'?

options.A: Preposition

questions.explanation: It is a preposition because it takes the noun phrase lunch as its complement.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'before' in 'Before you leave, call me'?

options.A: Subordinating conjunction

questions.explanation: It is a subordinating conjunction in traditional school grammar because it introduces the clause you leave.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'That is my bag'?

options.A: Demonstrative pronoun

questions.explanation: It is a demonstrative pronoun because it stands in place of a noun phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'That bag is mine'?

options.A: Demonstrative determiner/adjective

questions.explanation: It is a demonstrative determiner/adjective because it modifies the noun bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'I know that he is honest'?

options.A: Subordinating conjunction introducing a noun clause in traditional school grammar

questions.explanation: It is a subordinating conjunction introducing a noun clause in traditional school grammar.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'She sings well'?

options.A: Adverb

questions.explanation: It is an adverb because it modifies the verb sings.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'I am well'?

options.A: Adjective meaning healthy

questions.explanation: It is an adjective meaning healthy.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'The well is deep'?

options.A: Noun naming a water source

questions.explanation: It is a noun naming a water source.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between an adjective and an adverb?

options.A: An adjective generally modifies a noun or pronoun; an adverb generally modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or clause
options.B: An adjective modifies a verb; an adverb modifies a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective generally modifies a noun or pronoun; an adverb generally modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or clause. Compare: 'a careful driver' and 'drives carefully.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a noun and a pronoun?

options.A: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands in place of a noun or noun phrase
options.B: A noun stands in place of a pronoun; a pronoun names a person or place
options.C: Both name a person or place

questions.explanation: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands in place of a noun or noun phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a preposition and a conjunction?

options.A: A preposition normally takes a noun phrase or pronoun as its complement; a conjunction connects grammatical units and a subordinating conjunction introduces a clause
options.B: A preposition introduces a clause; a conjunction takes a noun phrase

questions.explanation: A preposition normally takes a noun phrase or pronoun as its complement; a conjunction connects grammatical units and a subordinating conjunction introduces a clause. Compare 'before lunch' and 'before lunch ended.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a conjunction and a conjunctive adverb?

options.A: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb expresses a relationship between clauses but is punctuated as an adverb
options.B: A conjunction expresses a relationship but is punctuated as an adverb; a conjunctive adverb connects clauses grammatically

questions.explanation: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb expresses a relationship between clauses but is punctuated as an adverb. Example: 'It rained, so we stayed in'; 'It rained; therefore, we stayed in.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a determiner and an adjective?

options.A: A determiner specifies or limits a noun phrase; an adjective describes a property
options.B: A determiner describes a property; an adjective specifies or limits a noun phrase

questions.explanation: A determiner specifies or limits a noun phrase (for example, the, a, this, my, some); an adjective describes a property (for example, beautiful, old, useful). Traditional school grammar may label some determiners as adjectives.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a gerund and a noun ending in -ing?

options.A: A gerund is a verb form functioning as a noun and can retain verbal properties, such as taking an object; a derived noun such as building may name a thing or result
options.B: A gerund names a thing; a derived noun retains verbal properties

questions.explanation: A gerund is a verb form functioning as a noun and can retain verbal properties, such as taking an object ('Reading books is useful'). A derived noun such as building may name a thing or result ('The building is tall').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: discuss about the issue

questions.explanation: 'Discuss the issue' is standard; discuss is transitive and does not normally take about before its direct object.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: return back

questions.explanation: Use return when it means come or go back; back is usually redundant in this expression.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: more preferable

questions.explanation: Preferable already expresses preference; in standard exam usage, avoid the redundant more preferable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: one of the student

questions.explanation: 'One of the students' is correct. One of is followed by a plural noun; the main verb agrees with one when it is the subject: 'One of the students is absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: each of the boys are

questions.explanation: 'Each of the boys is' is correct because each is singular.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression in traditional formal examination grammar?

options.A: Neither of the answers are correct.
options.B: Neither of the answers is correct.
options.C: Neither of the answers were correct.
options.D: Neither of the answers have correct.

questions.explanation: Traditional formal examination grammar generally expects 'Neither of the answers is correct.' In informal usage, plural agreement is sometimes found, but singular is the safer exam choice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The sceneries are beautiful.

questions.explanation: 'The scenery is beautiful' is standard because scenery is normally uncountable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: an advice

questions.explanation: 'A piece of advice' is correct because advice is uncountable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: many information

questions.explanation: 'Much information' is correct because information is uncountable; 'many pieces of information' is also correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression in careful formal usage?

options.A: less people

questions.explanation: In careful formal usage, use fewer people because people is countable. Use less with uncountable quantities: less water.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: between you and I

questions.explanation: 'Between you and me' is correct because the pronoun is the object of the preposition between.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: He is senior than me.

questions.explanation: 'He is senior to me' is correct. Senior, junior, superior and inferior are commonly followed by to, not than.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the safest standard form for formal examinations?

options.A: different than

questions.explanation: Different from is the safest standard form for formal examinations. Different than also occurs, especially in some varieties and constructions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: prefer coffee than tea

questions.explanation: 'Prefer coffee to tea' is the standard construction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression when referring to ability or skill?

options.A: good in English

questions.explanation: 'Good at English' is the usual expression when referring to ability or skill.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression when referring to a person?

options.A: He is angry on me.

questions.explanation: 'Angry with me' is the usual form when referring to a person; angry about or at can refer to a situation or matter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: I have been here since two hours.
options.B: I have been here for two hours.
options.C: I have been here from two hours.
options.D: I have been here at two hours.

questions.explanation: 'For two hours' is correct because it expresses duration. Use since with a starting point, such as since 6 a.m.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: He did not went.

questions.explanation: 'He did not go' is correct because did carries the past tense and is followed by the base form of the main verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: She can sings.

questions.explanation: 'She can sing' is correct because a modal auxiliary is followed by the base form of the verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: I look forward to meet you.
options.B: I look forward to meeting you.
options.C: I look forward to met you.
options.D: I look forward to meets you.

questions.explanation: 'I look forward to meeting you' is correct because to in this expression is a preposition and is followed by a gerund.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: despite of the rain

questions.explanation: 'Despite the rain' is correct. Do not add of after despite; use in spite of.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: Although he was tired, but he worked.
options.B: Although he was tired, he worked.
options.C: Although he was tired, and he worked.
options.D: Although he was tired, so he worked.

questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired, he worked' is correct. Do not normally use although and but together to join the same clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: For the meaning 'if you do not work', which expression is correct?

options.A: Unless you do not work...

questions.explanation: For the meaning 'if you do not work', use 'Unless you work...' Avoid an unnecessary second negative.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The furniture are new.

questions.explanation: 'The furniture is new' is correct because furniture is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The police is investigating.

questions.explanation: 'The police are investigating' is standard because police normally takes a plural verb. The singular expression is a police officer.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The cattle is grazing.

questions.explanation: 'The cattle are grazing' is standard because cattle is a plural noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: A number of applicants is waiting.
options.B: A number of applicants are waiting.
options.C: A number of applicants was waiting.
options.D: A number of applicants has waiting.

questions.explanation: 'A number of applicants are waiting' is correct because a number of means several and takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The number of applicants are increasing.
options.B: The number of applicants is increasing.
options.C: The number of applicants were increasing.
options.D: The number of applicants have increasing.

questions.explanation: 'The number of applicants is increasing' is correct because the subject is the singular phrase the number.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the nouns in 'Honesty is the best policy.'

options.A: Honesty and policy; honesty is abstract

questions.explanation: Honesty and policy are nouns; honesty is abstract.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the pronouns in 'They invited us.'

options.A: They and us; they is the subject form and us is the object form

questions.explanation: They and us are personal pronouns; they is the subject form and us is the object form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the verb in 'The children are playing.'

options.A: Are playing is the verb phrase; are is the auxiliary and playing is the main verb in the present participle form

questions.explanation: Are playing is the verb phrase; are is the auxiliary and playing is the main verb in the present participle form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the adjective in 'She bought a beautiful dress.'

options.A: Beautiful

questions.explanation: Beautiful is an adjective modifying the noun dress.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the adverb in 'He answered the question correctly.'

options.A: Correctly

questions.explanation: Correctly is an adverb modifying the verb answered.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the preposition in 'The keys are under the pillow.'

options.A: under

questions.explanation: Under is a preposition showing place.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the preposition in 'The keys are under the pillow.'

options.A: under

questions.explanation: Under is a preposition showing place.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the conjunction in 'I wanted to go, but it was raining.'

options.A: but

questions.explanation: But is a coordinating conjunction expressing contrast.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the interjection in 'Alas! We missed the train.'

options.A: Alas

questions.explanation: Alas is an interjection expressing sorrow or disappointment.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the articles in 'An owl sat on the tree.'

options.A: An is an indefinite article; the is a definite article
options.B: An is a definite article; the is an indefinite article

questions.explanation: An is an indefinite article; the is a definite article.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the parts of speech in 'The very intelligent student answered quickly.'

options.A: The is an article/determiner; very is an adverb; intelligent is an adjective; student is a noun; answered is a verb; quickly is an adverb
options.B: The is a verb; very is an adjective; intelligent is an adverb; student is a pronoun; answered is a noun; quickly is an adjective
options.C: The is a pronoun; very is a noun; intelligent is a verb; student is an adjective; answered is an adverb; quickly is a noun
options.D: The is a conjunction; very is a preposition; intelligent is a pronoun; student is a verb; answered is an adjective; quickly is a noun

questions.explanation: The is an article/determiner; very is an adverb; intelligent is an adjective; student is a noun; answered is a verb; quickly is an adverb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In error-spotting questions, which of the following should be checked?

options.A: Subject-verb agreement, countability, pronoun case, verb form, preposition choice, article use and parallelism

questions.explanation: In error-spotting questions, check subject-verb agreement, countability, pronoun case, verb form, preposition choice, article use and parallelism.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a common noun?

options.A: Ravi

questions.explanation: School names a class or kind of place rather than a particular individual, so it is a common noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an abstract noun?

options.A: stone

questions.explanation: Bravery names a quality that cannot usually be perceived through the five senses, so it is an abstract noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following nouns is normally uncountable?

options.A: furniture

questions.explanation: Furniture is normally uncountable; common uncountable nouns in examination questions include advice, information, furniture, luggage, baggage, equipment, machinery, knowledge, scenery, bread, traffic.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a plural-only noun?

options.A: book

questions.explanation: Scissors is a plural-only noun; other examples include trousers, spectacles, goods.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following nouns has the same singular and plural form?

options.A: sheep

questions.explanation: Sheep, deer, species and series have the same singular and plural forms.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'mouse'?

options.A: mouses

questions.explanation: Mouse is an irregular plural: mouse-mice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'goose'?

options.A: gooses

questions.explanation: Goose is an irregular plural: goose-geese.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the plural of 'foot'?

options.A: foots

questions.explanation: Foot is an irregular plural: foot-feet.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a material noun?

options.A: iron

questions.explanation: Iron names a substance or material from which things are made and is a material noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a collective noun?

options.A: herd

questions.explanation: Herd names a group considered as a unit and is a collective noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair shows nouns with the same form but different meanings in singular and plural?

options.A: work-works (employment-literary or artistic creations)

questions.explanation: Some nouns change meaning when pluralised. Examples: custom-customs (habit-duties/taxes), manner-manners (method-social behaviour), work-works (employment-literary or artistic creations).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a possessive pronoun?

options.A: my

questions.explanation: Mine is a possessive pronoun that stands independently. My is a possessive determiner.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive determiner?

options.A: This book is mine.

questions.explanation: A possessive determiner comes before a noun: 'This is my book.' Possessive pronouns replace the noun phrase: 'This book is mine.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a reflexive pronoun?

options.A: himself

questions.explanation: Himself is a reflexive pronoun; reflexive pronouns include myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses an emphatic pronoun?

options.A: He hurt himself.

questions.explanation: An emphatic pronoun merely adds emphasis and can be removed without making the basic sentence grammatically incomplete: 'He himself opened the gate.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun?

options.A: He himself opened the gate.

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is required to complete the intended meaning when it is the object: 'He hurt himself.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a demonstrative pronoun?

options.A: who

questions.explanation: These is a demonstrative pronoun; demonstrative pronouns are this, that, these, those.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'who' correctly as a subject form?

options.A: Whom came?

questions.explanation: Who is the subject form: 'Who came?' Whom is the object form: 'Whom did you meet?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'whom' correctly as an object form?

options.A: Whom came?

questions.explanation: Whom is the object form: 'Whom did you meet?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a relative pronoun?

options.A: which

questions.explanation: Which is a relative pronoun; relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, that.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which relative pronoun expresses possession?

options.A: who

questions.explanation: Whose expresses possession and can refer to people and, in formal usage, sometimes things.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which relative pronoun is not normally used after a comma in a non-defining clause?

options.A: who

questions.explanation: That commonly introduces defining relative clauses and is not normally used after a comma in a non-defining clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an indefinite pronoun?

options.A: someone

questions.explanation: Someone is an indefinite pronoun; indefinite pronouns include someone, somebody, anyone, anybody, everyone, everybody, no one, nothing, something, few, many, several, all, some, none.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which indefinite pronoun normally takes a singular verb?

options.A: both

questions.explanation: Everybody, everyone, somebody, anyone, each, either, neither normally take singular verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which indefinite pronoun normally takes a plural verb?

options.A: each

questions.explanation: Both, few, many, several take plural verbs.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a distributive pronoun?

options.A: each

questions.explanation: Each, either and neither are distributive pronouns. They normally take singular verbs when used as pronouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a reciprocal pronoun?

options.A: each other

questions.explanation: The reciprocal pronouns are each other and one another.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the antecedent of 'his' in 'Ravi lost his pen'?

options.A: Ravi

questions.explanation: In 'Ravi lost his pen,' Ravi is the antecedent of his.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct pronoun-antecedent agreement?

options.A: The girls brought their books.

questions.explanation: A pronoun should agree with its antecedent in number and, where relevant, person and gender: 'The girls brought their books.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a modal auxiliary verb?

options.A: be

questions.explanation: Must is a modal auxiliary. Common modals are can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a primary auxiliary?

options.A: can

questions.explanation: The primary auxiliaries are be, have and do. Can, must and should are modal auxiliaries.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a finite verb?

options.A: She works here.

questions.explanation: A finite verb is marked for tense and/or agreement with the subject: 'She works here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-finite verb form?

options.A: works

questions.explanation: The main non-finite forms are infinitives, gerunds and participles. 'To read' is an infinitive.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a transitive verb?

options.A: The baby slept.

questions.explanation: A transitive verb takes a direct object: 'She opened the door.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains an intransitive verb?

options.A: She opened the door.

questions.explanation: An intransitive verb does not take a direct object: 'The baby slept.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a ditransitive verb?

options.A: She opened the door.

questions.explanation: A ditransitive verb can take an indirect object and a direct object: 'He gave me a pen.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a linking verb?

options.A: She opened the door.

questions.explanation: A linking verb connects the subject to a subject complement that describes or identifies it: 'The soup tastes delicious.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a regular verb?

options.A: go-went-gone

questions.explanation: A regular verb forms its simple past and past participle by adding -ed or -d: work-worked-worked.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an irregular verb?

options.A: work-worked-worked

questions.explanation: An irregular verb does not form its past and past participle by the regular -ed pattern: go-went-gone.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a phrasal verb?

options.A: give up

questions.explanation: A phrasal verb is a combination of a verb and one or more particles that functions as a unit: give up (quit), look after (care for), put off (postpone), carry out (perform).

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a bare infinitive?

options.A: to read

questions.explanation: A bare infinitive appears without to after many modal verbs and certain verbs: 'She can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the present perfect tense?

options.A: I have completed the work.

questions.explanation: The present perfect tense links a past action or experience to the present. Form: has/have + past participle: 'I have completed the work.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the present perfect continuous tense?

options.A: They have been waiting for an hour.
options.C: They are waiting for an hour.
options.D: They will wait for an hour.

questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous emphasises an action that began in the past and continues up to the present or has a present result. Form: has/have been + verb-ing: 'They have been waiting for an hour.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the past perfect tense?

options.A: The train had left before we arrived.
options.B: The train left before we arrived.
options.C: The train has left before we arrived.
options.D: The train will leave before we arrive.

questions.explanation: The past perfect indicates an action completed before another past action or time. Form: had + past participle: 'The train had left before we arrived.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the past perfect continuous tense?

options.A: She had been working for two hours before the meeting began.
options.B: She was working for two hours before the meeting began.
options.C: She has been working for two hours before the meeting began.
options.D: She will have been working for two hours before the meeting began.

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action continuing up to a point in the past. Form: had been + verb-ing: 'She had been working for two hours before the meeting began.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the future perfect tense?

options.A: By Monday, she will have finished the report.
options.B: By Monday, she will finish the report.
options.C: By Monday, she will be finishing the report.
options.D: By Monday, she has finished the report.

questions.explanation: The future perfect describes an action that will be completed before a specified future time. Form: will have + past participle: 'By Monday, she will have finished the report.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the future perfect continuous tense?

options.A: By June, he will have been working here for ten years.
options.B: By June, he will work here for ten years.
options.C: By June, he will be working here for ten years.
options.D: By June, he has been working here for ten years.

questions.explanation: The future perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action up to a specified future point. Form: will have been + verb-ing: 'By June, he will have been working here for ten years.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct subject-verb agreement?

options.A: He work.

questions.explanation: The verb must agree with its subject in person and number: 'He works'; 'They work.' Both C and D are correct forms, but C is the singular agreement example given in the notes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with two subjects joined by 'and'?

options.A: Ravi and Rani is ready.

questions.explanation: A plural verb is normally used with two subjects joined by and: 'Ravi and Rani are ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows a fixed unit taking a singular verb?

options.A: Bread and butter are my usual breakfast.
options.B: Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.
options.C: Bread and butter were my usual breakfast.
options.D: Bread and butter have my usual breakfast.

questions.explanation: A single idea or a fixed unit may take a singular verb: 'Bread and butter is my usual breakfast.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with either...or?

options.A: Either the manager or the workers is coming.
options.B: Either the manager or the workers are coming.
options.C: Either the manager or the workers was coming.
options.D: Either the manager or the workers has coming.

questions.explanation: When either...or joins two subjects, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: 'Either the manager or the workers are coming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with neither...nor?

options.A: Neither the students nor the teacher are ready.
options.B: Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.
options.C: Neither the students nor the teacher were ready.
options.D: Neither the students nor the teacher have ready.

questions.explanation: When neither...nor joins two subjects, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with 'every'?

options.A: Every student have a book.
options.C: Every student are having a book.
options.D: Every student were having a book.

questions.explanation: Each, every, either and neither as the subject normally take a singular verb: 'Every student has a book.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with an intervening phrase?

options.A: The list of items are on the desk.
options.B: The list of items is on the desk.
options.C: The list of items were on the desk.
options.D: The list of items have on the desk.

questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the grammatical subject, not with a noun inside an intervening phrase: 'The list of items is on the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with a collective noun viewed as one unit?

options.A: The committee have reached its decision.
options.B: The committee has reached its decision.
options.C: The committee are reached its decision.
options.D: The committee were reached its decision.

questions.explanation: A collective noun can take a singular verb when the group is viewed as one unit: 'The committee has reached its decision.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with 'news'?

options.A: The news are encouraging.

questions.explanation: News, mathematics and physics normally take a singular verb: 'The news is encouraging.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with 'mathematics'?

options.A: Mathematics are difficult.

questions.explanation: News, mathematics and physics normally take a singular verb: 'Mathematics is difficult.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with 'a pair of trousers'?

options.A: A pair of trousers are missing.
options.B: A pair of trousers is missing.
options.C: A pair of trousers were missing.
options.D: A pair of trousers have missing.

questions.explanation: The expression a pair of takes a singular verb: 'A pair of trousers is missing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adjective of quality?

options.A: brave

questions.explanation: An adjective of quality describes the nature or quality of a noun: brave soldier, honest person, difficult question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adjective of quantity?

options.A: several

questions.explanation: An adjective of quantity indicates an amount of an uncountable noun: some water, little milk, enough food, much time.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adjective of number?

options.A: much

questions.explanation: An adjective of number indicates number or order: three books, several students, first prize, many people.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the comparative form of 'happy'?

options.A: happyer

questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in consonant + y change y to i and add -er/-est: happy-happier-happiest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the superlative form of 'big'?

options.A: biger

questions.explanation: A final consonant after a short stressed vowel is often doubled before -er/-est: big-bigger-biggest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the comparative form of 'beautiful'?

options.A: beautifuler

questions.explanation: Many longer adjectives use more and most: beautiful-more beautiful-most beautiful.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly compares two things?

options.A: Of the two plans, this one is best.
options.B: Of the two plans, this one is better.
options.C: Of the two plans, this one is good.
options.D: Of the two plans, this one is more best.

questions.explanation: Use the comparative degree, not the superlative, for two things: 'Of the two plans, this one is better.'
