questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as...as'?

options.A: She is as taller as her sister.
options.B: She is as tall as her sister.
options.C: She is as tallest as her sister.
options.D: She is as more tall as her sister.

questions.explanation: Use the positive degree between as and as: 'She is as tall as her sister.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not so/as...as'?

options.A: This road is not as wider as that road.
options.B: This road is not as wide as that road.
options.C: This road is not as widest as that road.
options.D: This road is not as more wide as that road.

questions.explanation: Not so/as...as expresses inequality using the positive degree: 'This road is not as wide as that road.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence follows the usual order of adjectives?

options.A: a brown small old round beautiful Italian wooden dining table
options.B: a beautiful small old round brown Italian wooden dining table
options.C: a wooden beautiful small old round brown Italian dining table
options.D: a round brown small beautiful old Italian wooden dining table

questions.explanation: A common order is opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose and then the noun: 'a beautiful small old round brown Italian wooden dining table.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of coordinate adjectives?

options.A: three large wooden boxes

questions.explanation: Coordinate adjectives independently modify the same noun and can often be joined by and or separated by commas: 'a long, difficult examination.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of cumulative adjectives?

options.A: a long, difficult examination

questions.explanation: Cumulative adjectives build meaning in a fixed order and are not normally separated by commas: 'three large wooden boxes.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a postpositive adjective?

options.A: a beautiful garden

questions.explanation: A postpositive adjective follows the noun or pronoun it modifies, often in fixed expressions or formal usage: 'something useful'; 'the people responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of manner?

options.A: here

questions.explanation: An adverb of manner tells how an action is performed: slowly, carefully, well, politely.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of place?

options.A: outside

questions.explanation: An adverb of place tells where an action occurs: here, there, outside, nearby, everywhere.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of time?

options.A: always

questions.explanation: An adverb of time tells when an action occurs: now, yesterday, soon, later, already.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of frequency?

options.A: often

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency tells how often an action occurs: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of degree?

options.A: here

questions.explanation: An adverb of degree tells the intensity or extent of an action, adjective or adverb: very, too, quite, almost, extremely, enough.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an adverb of affirmation or negation?

options.A: certainly

questions.explanation: An adverb of affirmation or negation expresses confirmation or denial: certainly, surely, definitely, not, never.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a sentence adverb?

options.A: She spoke politely.
options.B: Fortunately, the train arrived on time.

questions.explanation: A sentence adverb comments on the whole sentence or the speaker's attitude: 'Fortunately, the train arrived on time'; 'Honestly, I disagree.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an interrogative adverb?

options.A: when

questions.explanation: An interrogative adverb asks a question about time, place, manner or reason: when, where, how, why.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a relative adverb?

options.A: I remember the day when we met.

questions.explanation: A relative adverb introduces a clause and relates it to a time, place or reason: when, where, why. Example: 'I remember the day when we met.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the adverb of frequency with an ordinary main verb?

options.A: She visits often us.

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency usually appears before an ordinary main verb: 'She often visits us.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the adverb of frequency with the verb 'be'?

options.A: She always is punctual.

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency usually appears after the finite form of be: 'She is always punctual.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the adverb of frequency with an auxiliary verb?

options.A: They never have visited Delhi.

questions.explanation: An adverb of frequency generally appears after the first auxiliary: 'They have never visited Delhi.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'enough' with an adjective?

options.A: He is enough old to drive.
options.B: He is old enough to drive.
options.C: He is old to drive enough.
options.D: Enough he is old to drive.

questions.explanation: Enough normally follows the adjective or adverb: old enough; quickly enough.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'enough' with a noun?

options.A: We have time enough.
options.C: We have time enough to spare.

questions.explanation: Enough normally comes before the noun: enough time; enough money.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'so' correctly?

options.A: She is so beautiful.
options.B: She is so a beautiful place.

questions.explanation: So usually modifies an adjective or adverb: 'She is so beautiful.' Such modifies a noun phrase: 'such a beautiful place.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'such' correctly?

options.A: It was such a beautiful place.
options.C: It was so a beautiful place.

questions.explanation: Such modifies a noun phrase: 'such a beautiful place.' So usually modifies an adjective or adverb: 'so beautiful.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a preposition of place?

options.A: under

questions.explanation: Under is a preposition of place indicating location or position. Since is a preposition of time; towards is a preposition of direction; because of is a phrase preposition.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a preposition of time?

options.A: between

questions.explanation: Since is a preposition of time. Between and in front of are prepositions of place; into is a preposition of direction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a preposition of direction or movement?

options.A: during

questions.explanation: Through is a preposition of direction or movement. During and for are prepositions of time; beside is a preposition of place.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'by' to indicate the agent in a passive sentence?

options.A: The letter was written by Ravi.
options.B: The letter was written with Ravi.
options.C: The letter was written at Ravi.
options.D: The letter was written in Ravi.

questions.explanation: By commonly indicates the agent in a passive sentence: 'The letter was written by Ravi.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'with' to indicate an instrument?

options.A: She cut it by a knife.
options.B: She cut it with a knife.
options.C: She cut it at a knife.
options.D: She cut it on a knife.

questions.explanation: With commonly indicates an instrument: 'She cut it with a knife.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a simple preposition?

options.A: in front of

questions.explanation: A simple preposition consists of one word, such as in, on, at, by, for, from, with.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a compound preposition?

options.A: in

questions.explanation: A compound preposition is formed from more than one element or a prefixed form, such as inside, outside, within, without, into, upon.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a phrase preposition?

options.A: in

questions.explanation: A phrase preposition is a group of words functioning as a preposition. Examples: because of, in front of, in spite of, according to, on behalf of, with regard to.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'at' for time?

options.A: We will meet at Monday.

questions.explanation: At is used for precise clock times and certain fixed expressions: at 6 p.m., at noon, at midnight, at night.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'on' for time?

options.A: We will meet on 6 p.m.

questions.explanation: On is used with days and dates: on Monday, on 15 August, on my birthday.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in' for time?

options.A: We will meet in 6 p.m.

questions.explanation: In is used with months, years, seasons, centuries and longer periods: in July, in 2026, in winter, in the 21st century.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'at' for place?

options.A: She is at the bus stop.

questions.explanation: At commonly indicates a point or specific location: at the bus stop, at the entrance, at school.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'in' for place?

options.A: She is in the bus stop.

questions.explanation: In indicates being inside an enclosed space or within an area: in the room, in Bengaluru, in India.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'on' for place?

options.A: The book is on the room.
options.B: The book is on the table.
options.D: The book is on the bus stop.

questions.explanation: On indicates a surface or position along a line or route: on the table, on the wall, on the road.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: because

questions.explanation: But is one of the seven coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). Because, although and unless are subordinating conjunctions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which acronym is used to remember the seven coordinating conjunctions?

options.A: FANBOYS

questions.explanation: The seven common coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so, often remembered by the acronym FANBOYS.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'nor'?

options.A: He did not call, nor did he write.
options.B: He did not call, nor he wrote.
options.C: He did not call, nor he did write.
options.D: He did not call, nor wrote he.

questions.explanation: Nor adds a negative alternative and commonly follows a negative statement or neither: 'He did not call, nor did he write.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'yet' as a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: The task was difficult, yet she completed it.
options.B: The task was difficult, yet she completed it not.
options.C: The task was difficult, yet she did not completed it.
options.D: The task was difficult, yet she not completed it.

questions.explanation: Yet expresses contrast or an unexpected result: 'The task was difficult, yet she completed it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so' as a coordinating conjunction?

options.A: It was raining, so we stayed indoors.
options.B: It was raining, so we stayed indoors not.
options.C: It was raining, so we did not stayed indoors.
options.D: It was raining, so we not stayed indoors.

questions.explanation: So can express a result: 'It was raining, so we stayed indoors.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'for' as a conjunction?

options.A: I stayed indoors, for it was raining.
options.B: I stayed indoors, for it was raining not.
options.C: I stayed indoors, for it did not rained.
options.D: I stayed indoors, for it not rained.

questions.explanation: For can introduce a reason in a formal or literary style: 'I stayed indoors, for it was raining.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a pair of correlative conjunctions?

options.A: both...and

questions.explanation: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or, rather...than.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct parallelism with correlative conjunctions?

options.A: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
options.B: She is not only intelligent but also hardwork.
options.C: She is not only intelligence but also hardworking.
options.D: She is not only intelligent but also hardworks.

questions.explanation: The grammatical forms after both parts of the pair should be balanced: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct parallelism with 'both...and'?

options.A: He likes both reading and writing.
options.B: He likes both reading and to write.
options.C: He likes both read and writing.
options.D: He likes both to read and write.

questions.explanation: The grammatical forms after both parts of the pair should be balanced: 'He likes both reading and writing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a conjunctive adverb?

options.A: and

questions.explanation: A conjunctive adverb connects ideas between clauses or sentences and expresses a logical relationship. Examples: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise, furthermore. It is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a conjunctive adverb joining independent clauses?

options.A: The road was blocked; therefore, we took another route.
options.B: The road was blocked, therefore we took another route.
options.C: The road was blocked therefore; we took another route.
options.D: The road was blocked: therefore we took another route.

questions.explanation: Use a semicolon before a conjunctive adverb and a comma after it: 'The road was blocked; therefore, we took another route.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'although'?

options.A: Although it rained, we played.
options.C: Although it rained, but we played.
options.D: Although the rain, but we played.

questions.explanation: Although is a conjunction followed by a clause: 'Although it rained, we played.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'despite'?

options.A: Despite the rain, we played.
options.C: Despite of the rain, we played.
options.D: Despite the rain, but we played.

questions.explanation: Despite is a preposition followed by a noun phrase or gerund: 'Despite the rain, we played.' Do not add of after despite; use in spite of.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because'?

options.A: She stayed home because she was ill.
options.B: She stayed home because of she was ill.
options.C: She stayed home because her illness.
options.D: She stayed home because of her was ill.

questions.explanation: Because is a conjunction followed by a clause: 'She stayed home because she was ill.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'because of'?

options.A: She stayed home because of her illness.
options.B: She stayed home because of she was ill.
options.C: She stayed home because her illness.
options.D: She stayed home because of she is ill.

questions.explanation: Because of is a prepositional expression followed by a noun phrase or gerund: 'She stayed home because of her illness.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'so...that'?

options.A: He was so tired that he slept immediately.
options.B: He was so tired that he sleep immediately.
options.C: He was such tired that he slept immediately.
options.D: He was so a tired that he slept immediately.

questions.explanation: So is followed by an adjective/adverb and that clause: 'so tired that he slept.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'such...that'?

options.A: It was such a difficult task that we needed help.
options.B: It was so a difficult task that we needed help.
options.C: It was such difficult that we needed help.
options.D: It was such a difficult that we needed help.

questions.explanation: Such is followed by a noun phrase and that clause: 'such a difficult task that we needed help.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is an independent clause?

options.A: A clause that can stand alone as a complete sentence
options.B: A clause that cannot stand alone
options.C: A group of words without a verb

questions.explanation: An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a dependent clause?

options.A: A clause that cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence
options.B: A clause that can always stand alone
options.C: A group of words without a verb

questions.explanation: A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a simple sentence?

options.A: She sings.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence contains one independent clause: 'She sings.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a compound sentence?

options.A: She sings.

questions.explanation: A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses, commonly joined by a coordinating conjunction or separated by a semicolon: 'She sings, and he dances.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a complex sentence?

options.A: She sings.

questions.explanation: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause: 'Although she sings, he dances.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a' based on sound?

options.A: She is a university student.

questions.explanation: Use a university because it begins with the /ju/ consonant sound. Use an hour because the h is silent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'an' based on sound?

options.A: He is a honest man.

questions.explanation: Use an before a vowel sound: an honest man (the h is silent), an hour, an MBA graduate.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly applies the first-mention and second-mention rule?

options.A: I saw a dog. The dog was black.
options.B: I saw the dog. A dog was black.
options.C: I saw a dog. A dog was black.
options.D: I saw the dog. The dog was black.

questions.explanation: A singular countable noun is often introduced with a/an and referred to later with the: 'I saw a dog. The dog was black.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with a unique thing?

options.A: The Sun rises in the east.
options.B: A Sun rises in the east.
options.D: An Sun rises in the east.

questions.explanation: Use the with entities understood as unique in the context: the Sun, the Moon, the Earth, the sky.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with a superlative adjective?

options.A: She is tallest girl in the class.
options.B: She is the tallest girl in the class.
options.C: She is a tallest girl in the class.
options.D: She is an tallest girl in the class.

questions.explanation: Use the before a superlative adjective in ordinary attributive use: the tallest building, the most useful book.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with an ordinal number?

options.A: Read first chapter.

questions.explanation: Use the in expressions such as the first chapter, the second question, the last day.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with a river?

options.A: The Ganga is a sacred river.
options.B: A Ganga is a sacred river.
options.D: An Ganga is a sacred river.

questions.explanation: Use the with names such as the Ganga, the Nile, the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly omits the article before a language?

options.A: She speaks the Kannada fluently.

questions.explanation: Articles are normally omitted when referring to languages and academic subjects generally: Kannada, English, mathematics, history.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly omits the article before a meal referred to generally?

options.A: We have the breakfast at eight.
options.B: We have a breakfast at eight.
options.D: We have an breakfast at eight.

questions.explanation: Articles are commonly omitted when meals are referred to generally: 'We have breakfast at eight.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses no article for general reference?

options.A: The books are useful.

questions.explanation: Use no article for general reference: 'Books are useful'; 'Water is essential.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' for a specific group?

options.A: Books on this shelf are mine.
options.B: The books on this shelf are mine.
options.C: A books on this shelf are mine.
options.D: An books on this shelf are mine.

questions.explanation: Use the when referring to a specific group or amount: 'The books on this shelf are mine.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses an article with a profession?

options.A: She is doctor.

questions.explanation: Use a/an before a singular countable profession: 'She is a doctor'; 'He is an engineer.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the article with a musical instrument?

options.A: She plays a violin.

questions.explanation: In the traditional pattern for ability or performance, use the: 'She plays the violin.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the article with a newspaper title?

options.A: She reads a Hindu.

questions.explanation: Use the with newspaper titles when the title convention includes it, for example The Hindu and The Times of India.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly chooses a/an with an abbreviation based on sound?

options.A: He is a MLA.

questions.explanation: Choose a/an according to the initial spoken sound, not the written letter. Examples: an FIR (said 'ef...'), an MLA, a UNESCO body (if pronounced with /ju/), an X-ray.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly chooses 'a' with an abbreviation based on sound?

options.A: It is an UNESCO body.

questions.explanation: Choose a/an according to the initial spoken sound, not the written letter. A UNESCO body if pronounced with /ju/.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'an' with an abbreviation based on sound?

options.A: It is a FIR.

questions.explanation: Choose a/an according to the initial spoken sound, not the written letter. Examples: an FIR (said 'ef...'), an MLA, a UNESCO body (if pronounced with /ju/), an X-ray.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a' with an abbreviation based on sound?

options.A: It is an X-ray.

questions.explanation: X-ray is pronounced with an initial /e/ vowel sound, so 'an X-ray' is standard. UNESCO is pronounced with /ju/, so 'a UNESCO body' is standard. FIR is pronounced 'ef...', so 'an FIR' is standard. Among the options, only 'a X-ray' is incorrect. The intended answer key here is 'a UNESCO body' but that option is not listed; the closest correct-sound form among the options is 'It is a X-ray' only if X is read as a letter name beginning with a consonant sound in some conventions. Re-check: X-ray begins with the vowel sound /e/, so 'an X-ray' is correct. Therefore none of the options A-D is fully correct as written. The safe exam rule is: choose a/an by spoken sound.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which expression correctly uses 'a few'?

options.A: A few students understood the lesson.

questions.explanation: A few means some and is used with plural countable nouns: 'A few students understood the lesson.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which expression correctly uses 'few'?

options.A: Few students understood the lesson.

questions.explanation: Few means almost none and is used with plural countable nouns: 'Few students understood the lesson.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which expression correctly uses 'a little'?

options.A: A little hope remains.
options.C: A little books are on the desk.

questions.explanation: A little means some and is used with uncountable nouns: 'There is a little hope.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which expression correctly uses 'little'?

options.A: There is little hope.

questions.explanation: Little means almost no amount and is used with uncountable nouns: 'There is little hope.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a number of'?

options.A: A number of students are absent.
options.B: A number of students is absent.
options.C: A number of student are absent.
options.D: A number of student is absent.

questions.explanation: A number of means several and takes a plural verb: 'A number of students are absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the number of'?

options.A: The number of students are increasing.
options.B: The number of students is increasing.
options.C: The number of student are increasing.
options.D: The number of student is increasing.

questions.explanation: The number of refers to the total and takes a singular verb: 'The number of students is increasing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'before' in 'Come before lunch'?

options.A: Preposition

questions.explanation: It is a preposition because it takes the noun phrase lunch as its complement.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'before' in 'Before you leave, call me'?

options.A: Subordinating conjunction

questions.explanation: It is a subordinating conjunction in traditional school grammar because it introduces the clause you leave.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'That is my bag'?

options.A: Demonstrative pronoun

questions.explanation: It is a demonstrative pronoun because it stands in place of a noun phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'That bag is mine'?

options.A: Demonstrative determiner/adjective

questions.explanation: It is a demonstrative determiner/adjective because it modifies the noun bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'that' in 'I know that he is honest'?

options.A: Subordinating conjunction introducing a noun clause in traditional school grammar

questions.explanation: It is a subordinating conjunction introducing a noun clause in traditional school grammar.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'She sings well'?

options.A: Adverb

questions.explanation: It is an adverb because it modifies the verb sings.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'I am well'?

options.A: Adjective meaning healthy

questions.explanation: It is an adjective meaning healthy.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'well' in 'The well is deep'?

options.A: Noun naming a water source

questions.explanation: It is a noun naming a water source.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between an adjective and an adverb?

options.A: An adjective generally modifies a noun or pronoun; an adverb generally modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or clause
options.B: An adjective modifies a verb; an adverb modifies a noun

questions.explanation: An adjective generally modifies a noun or pronoun; an adverb generally modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or clause. Compare: 'a careful driver' and 'drives carefully.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a noun and a pronoun?

options.A: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands in place of a noun or noun phrase
options.B: A noun stands in place of a pronoun; a pronoun names a person or place
options.C: Both name a person or place

questions.explanation: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands in place of a noun or noun phrase.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a preposition and a conjunction?

options.A: A preposition normally takes a noun phrase or pronoun as its complement; a conjunction connects grammatical units and a subordinating conjunction introduces a clause
options.B: A preposition introduces a clause; a conjunction takes a noun phrase

questions.explanation: A preposition normally takes a noun phrase or pronoun as its complement; a conjunction connects grammatical units and a subordinating conjunction introduces a clause. Compare 'before lunch' and 'before lunch ended.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a conjunction and a conjunctive adverb?

options.A: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb expresses a relationship between clauses but is punctuated as an adverb
options.B: A conjunction expresses a relationship but is punctuated as an adverb; a conjunctive adverb connects clauses grammatically

questions.explanation: A conjunction grammatically connects clauses; a conjunctive adverb expresses a relationship between clauses but is punctuated as an adverb. Example: 'It rained, so we stayed in'; 'It rained; therefore, we stayed in.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a determiner and an adjective?

options.A: A determiner specifies or limits a noun phrase; an adjective describes a property
options.B: A determiner describes a property; an adjective specifies or limits a noun phrase

questions.explanation: A determiner specifies or limits a noun phrase (for example, the, a, this, my, some); an adjective describes a property (for example, beautiful, old, useful). Traditional school grammar may label some determiners as adjectives.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between a gerund and a noun ending in -ing?

options.A: A gerund is a verb form functioning as a noun and can retain verbal properties, such as taking an object; a derived noun such as building may name a thing or result
options.B: A gerund names a thing; a derived noun retains verbal properties

questions.explanation: A gerund is a verb form functioning as a noun and can retain verbal properties, such as taking an object ('Reading books is useful'). A derived noun such as building may name a thing or result ('The building is tall').

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: discuss about the issue

questions.explanation: 'Discuss the issue' is standard; discuss is transitive and does not normally take about before its direct object.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: return back

questions.explanation: Use return when it means come or go back; back is usually redundant in this expression.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: more preferable

questions.explanation: Preferable already expresses preference; in standard exam usage, avoid the redundant more preferable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: one of the student

questions.explanation: 'One of the students' is correct. One of is followed by a plural noun; the main verb agrees with one when it is the subject: 'One of the students is absent.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: each of the boys are

questions.explanation: 'Each of the boys is' is correct because each is singular.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression in traditional formal examination grammar?

options.A: Neither of the answers are correct.
options.B: Neither of the answers is correct.
options.C: Neither of the answers were correct.
options.D: Neither of the answers have correct.

questions.explanation: Traditional formal examination grammar generally expects 'Neither of the answers is correct.' In informal usage, plural agreement is sometimes found, but singular is the safer exam choice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The sceneries are beautiful.

questions.explanation: 'The scenery is beautiful' is standard because scenery is normally uncountable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: an advice

questions.explanation: 'A piece of advice' is correct because advice is uncountable.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: many information

questions.explanation: 'Much information' is correct because information is uncountable; 'many pieces of information' is also correct.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression in careful formal usage?

options.A: less people

questions.explanation: In careful formal usage, use fewer people because people is countable. Use less with uncountable quantities: less water.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: between you and I

questions.explanation: 'Between you and me' is correct because the pronoun is the object of the preposition between.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: He is senior than me.

questions.explanation: 'He is senior to me' is correct. Senior, junior, superior and inferior are commonly followed by to, not than.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the safest standard form for formal examinations?

options.A: different than

questions.explanation: Different from is the safest standard form for formal examinations. Different than also occurs, especially in some varieties and constructions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: prefer coffee than tea

questions.explanation: 'Prefer coffee to tea' is the standard construction.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression when referring to ability or skill?

options.A: good in English

questions.explanation: 'Good at English' is the usual expression when referring to ability or skill.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression when referring to a person?

options.A: He is angry on me.

questions.explanation: 'Angry with me' is the usual form when referring to a person; angry about or at can refer to a situation or matter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: I have been here since two hours.
options.B: I have been here for two hours.
options.C: I have been here from two hours.
options.D: I have been here at two hours.

questions.explanation: 'For two hours' is correct because it expresses duration. Use since with a starting point, such as since 6 a.m.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: He did not went.

questions.explanation: 'He did not go' is correct because did carries the past tense and is followed by the base form of the main verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: She can sings.

questions.explanation: 'She can sing' is correct because a modal auxiliary is followed by the base form of the verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: I look forward to meet you.
options.B: I look forward to meeting you.
options.C: I look forward to met you.
options.D: I look forward to meets you.

questions.explanation: 'I look forward to meeting you' is correct because to in this expression is a preposition and is followed by a gerund.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: despite of the rain

questions.explanation: 'Despite the rain' is correct. Do not add of after despite; use in spite of.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: Although he was tired, but he worked.
options.B: Although he was tired, he worked.
options.C: Although he was tired, and he worked.
options.D: Although he was tired, so he worked.

questions.explanation: 'Although he was tired, he worked' is correct. Do not normally use although and but together to join the same clauses.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: For the meaning 'if you do not work', which expression is correct?

options.A: Unless you do not work...

questions.explanation: For the meaning 'if you do not work', use 'Unless you work...' Avoid an unnecessary second negative.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The furniture are new.

questions.explanation: 'The furniture is new' is correct because furniture is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The police is investigating.

questions.explanation: 'The police are investigating' is standard because police normally takes a plural verb. The singular expression is a police officer.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The cattle is grazing.

questions.explanation: 'The cattle are grazing' is standard because cattle is a plural noun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: A number of applicants is waiting.
options.B: A number of applicants are waiting.
options.C: A number of applicants was waiting.
options.D: A number of applicants has waiting.

questions.explanation: 'A number of applicants are waiting' is correct because a number of means several and takes a plural verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The number of applicants are increasing.
options.B: The number of applicants is increasing.
options.C: The number of applicants were increasing.
options.D: The number of applicants have increasing.

questions.explanation: 'The number of applicants is increasing' is correct because the subject is the singular phrase the number.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the nouns in 'Honesty is the best policy.'

options.A: Honesty and policy; honesty is abstract

questions.explanation: Honesty and policy are nouns; honesty is abstract.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the pronouns in 'They invited us.'

options.A: They and us; they is the subject form and us is the object form

questions.explanation: They and us are personal pronouns; they is the subject form and us is the object form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the verb in 'The children are playing.'

options.A: Are playing is the verb phrase; are is the auxiliary and playing is the main verb in the present participle form

questions.explanation: Are playing is the verb phrase; are is the auxiliary and playing is the main verb in the present participle form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the adjective in 'She bought a beautiful dress.'

options.A: Beautiful

questions.explanation: Beautiful is an adjective modifying the noun dress.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the adverb in 'He answered the question correctly.'

options.A: Correctly

questions.explanation: Correctly is an adverb modifying the verb answered.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the preposition in 'The keys are under the pillow.'

options.A: under

questions.explanation: Under is a preposition showing place.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the conjunction in 'I wanted to go, but it was raining.'

options.A: but

questions.explanation: But is a coordinating conjunction expressing contrast.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the interjection in 'Alas! We missed the train.'

options.A: Alas

questions.explanation: Alas is an interjection expressing sorrow or disappointment.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the articles in 'An owl sat on the tree.'

options.A: An is an indefinite article; the is a definite article
options.B: An is a definite article; the is an indefinite article

questions.explanation: An is an indefinite article; the is a definite article.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Identify the parts of speech in 'The very intelligent student answered quickly.'

options.A: The is an article/determiner; very is an adverb; intelligent is an adjective; student is a noun; answered is a verb; quickly is an adverb
options.B: The is a verb; very is an adjective; intelligent is an adverb; student is a pronoun; answered is a noun; quickly is an adjective
options.C: The is a pronoun; very is a noun; intelligent is a verb; student is an adjective; answered is an adverb; quickly is a noun
options.D: The is a conjunction; very is a preposition; intelligent is a pronoun; student is a verb; answered is an adjective; quickly is a noun

questions.explanation: The is an article/determiner; very is an adverb; intelligent is an adjective; student is a noun; answered is a verb; quickly is an adverb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In error-spotting questions, which of the following should be checked?

options.A: Subject-verb agreement, countability, pronoun case, verb form, preposition choice, article use and parallelism

questions.explanation: In error-spotting questions, check subject-verb agreement, countability, pronoun case, verb form, preposition choice, article use and parallelism.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following should be revised for noun types?

options.A: Countable/uncountable nouns, irregular plurals and possessive forms

questions.explanation: Revise noun types, countable/uncountable nouns, irregular plurals and possessive forms.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following should be revised for pronouns?

options.A: Pronoun cases, antecedent agreement, reflexive/emphatic forms and who/whom

questions.explanation: Revise pronoun cases, antecedent agreement, reflexive/emphatic forms and who/whom.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following should be learned for verbs?

options.A: Verb forms, auxiliaries, finite/non-finite verbs, transitive/intransitive verbs, tense patterns and subject-verb agreement

questions.explanation: Learn verb forms, auxiliaries, finite/non-finite verbs, transitive/intransitive verbs, tense patterns and subject-verb agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following should be practised for adjectives?

options.A: Adjective degrees, irregular comparisons and adjective order

questions.explanation: Practise adjective degrees, irregular comparisons and adjective order.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which confusing adverb pairs should be distinguished?

options.A: hard/hardly, late/lately and near/nearly

questions.explanation: Distinguish adverbs ending in -ly from adjectives, and learn confusing pairs such as hard/hardly, late/lately and near/nearly.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which high-frequency preposition distinctions should be memorised?

options.A: in/on/at, since/for and by/until

questions.explanation: Memorise high-frequency preposition combinations and the differences among in/on/at, since/for and by/until.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which conjunction topics should be learned?

options.A: FANBOYS, subordinating conjunctions, correlative conjunctions and parallel structure

questions.explanation: Learn FANBOYS, subordinating conjunctions, correlative conjunctions and parallel structure.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which article rules should be mastered?

options.A: a/an/the/zero article rules, especially sound-based a/an selection and geographical names

questions.explanation: Master a/an/the/zero article rules, especially sound-based a/an selection and geographical names.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What should be recognised regarding interjections?

options.A: Recognise interjections and their punctuation

questions.explanation: Recognise interjections and their punctuation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a noun phrase?

options.A: The tall boy in the blue shirt

questions.explanation: A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun or pronoun and functioning as a noun unit: 'The tall boy in the blue shirt' won the race.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'Swimming is good exercise,' what is 'Swimming'?

options.A: A gerund used as a noun
options.B: A present participle used as an adjective

questions.explanation: A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun: 'Swimming is good exercise.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a verbal noun?

options.A: arrival

questions.explanation: A verbal noun is a noun formed from a verb and used as a noun, often naming an action or result: arrival, decision, movement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'The boiling water is hot,' what is 'boiling'?

options.A: A present participle used as an adjective
options.B: A gerund used as a noun

questions.explanation: A present participle is the -ing form used in progressive verb phrases or as an adjective: 'the boiling water.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'She is swimming,' what is 'swimming'?

options.A: A present participle forming a progressive verb
options.B: A gerund used as a noun

questions.explanation: A present participle forms a progressive verb: 'She is swimming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'Swimming is healthy,' what is 'Swimming'?

options.A: A gerund functioning as a noun
options.B: A present participle forming a progressive verb

questions.explanation: A gerund functions as a noun: 'Swimming is healthy.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a bare infinitive?

options.A: She can swim.

questions.explanation: A bare infinitive appears without to after many modal verbs and certain verbs: 'She can swim.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a past participle?

options.A: The window was broken.

questions.explanation: A past participle is the third principal form of a verb, used in perfect tenses, passive constructions and adjective-like uses: 'The window was broken.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the simple present tense?

options.A: The earth revolves around the Sun.
options.B: The earth is revolving around the Sun.
options.C: The earth revolved around the Sun.
options.D: The earth will revolve around the Sun.

questions.explanation: The simple present tense is used for habits, routines, general truths, facts and scheduled events: 'The earth revolves around the Sun.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the present continuous tense?

options.A: She is studying.

questions.explanation: The present continuous tense is used for actions happening now, temporary situations and arranged future events. Form: am/is/are + verb-ing: 'She is studying.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the simple past tense?

options.A: She visited Mysuru yesterday.

questions.explanation: The simple past tense describes a completed action or state in the past: 'She visited Mysuru yesterday.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the past continuous tense?

options.A: I was reading when he called.
options.C: I am reading when he called.
options.D: I will read when he called.

questions.explanation: The past continuous tense describes an action in progress at a particular past time or an ongoing action interrupted by another. Form: was/were + verb-ing: 'I was reading when he called.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the simple future tense?

options.A: I will call you tomorrow.

questions.explanation: The simple future tense commonly expresses a future prediction, decision or willingness. Form: will + base verb: 'I will call you tomorrow.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence is in the future continuous tense?

options.A: At 8 p.m., I will be studying.

questions.explanation: The future continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at a particular future time. Form: will be + verb-ing: 'At 8 p.m., I will be studying.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'between' with more than two items?

options.A: The prize was divided between the three candidates.
options.B: The prize was divided among the three candidates only.
options.C: The prize was divided between among the candidates.
options.D: The prize was divided among the two candidates.

questions.explanation: Between is traditionally used for distinct, individually considered items (including more than two): 'between the three candidates.' Among is used for a group or mass.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'among'?

options.A: She was lost among the crowd.
options.B: She was lost between the crowd.
options.C: She was lost among the two friends.
options.D: She was lost between the two friends.

questions.explanation: Among is used for a group or mass: 'among the crowd.' Between is used for distinct, individually considered items.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'unless'?

options.A: Unless you study, you may fail.
options.B: Unless you do not study, you may fail.
options.C: Unless you will not study, you may fail.
options.D: Unless you did not study, you may fail.

questions.explanation: Unless means 'except if' or 'if not'. Avoid adding another negative when it creates an unintended double negative: 'Unless you study, you may fail.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly contrasts two facts using 'whereas'?

options.A: Ravi is tall, whereas Mohan is short.
options.B: Ravi is tall, whereas Mohan is short not.
options.C: Ravi is tall, whereas Mohan short.
options.D: Ravi is tall, whereas Mohan did not short.

questions.explanation: Whereas is used mainly to contrast two facts: 'Ravi is tall, whereas Mohan is short.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'while' to indicate simultaneous time?

options.A: While I was reading, the phone rang.
options.B: While I was reading, the phone ring.
options.C: While I was reading, the phone did not ring.
options.D: While I read, the phone was rang.

questions.explanation: While can indicate simultaneous time: 'While I was reading, the phone rang.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'as' to introduce a reason treated as background information?

options.A: As it was raining, we stayed indoors.
options.B: As it was raining, we stayed indoors not.
options.C: As it was raining, but we stayed indoors.
options.D: As it was raining, so we stayed indoors.

questions.explanation: As often introduces a reason treated as background information: 'As it was raining, we stayed indoors.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains an interjection of joy?

options.A: Hurrah! We won the match.

questions.explanation: Hurrah! is a common interjection of joy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains an interjection of pain?

options.A: Hurrah! We won the match.

questions.explanation: Ouch! is a common interjection of pain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence contains a milder interruption using a comma after the interjection?

options.A: Well, let us begin.

questions.explanation: A comma may be used for a milder interruption: 'Well, let us begin.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the zero article with a proper name?

options.A: Ravi is here.

questions.explanation: Articles are normally omitted before personal names: 'Ravi is here,' not ordinarily 'the Ravi is here.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'a' with a profession?

options.A: He is an engineer.

questions.explanation: Use a/an before a singular countable profession: 'She is a doctor'; 'He is an engineer.'

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'The bag is light'?

options.A: Adjective

questions.explanation: It is an adjective because it describes the bag.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'Please light the lamp'?

options.A: Verb

questions.explanation: It is a verb because it expresses an action.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'light' in 'Turn on the light'?

options.A: Noun

questions.explanation: It is a noun because it names a thing.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'fast' in 'He drives fast'?

options.A: Adverb

questions.explanation: It is an adverb because it modifies the verb drives.

questions.subject: English
questions.chapter: Words That Change Part of Speech
questions.question: What part of speech is 'fast' in 'He is a fast runner'?

options.A: Adjective

questions.explanation: It is an adjective because it modifies the noun runner.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct object form after a preposition?

options.A: This gift is for I.

questions.explanation: Use the object form after a preposition: for me, with him, between us, to them.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct subject form?

options.A: Him is going to the market.
options.B: He is going to the market.
options.C: His is going to the market.
options.D: Himself is going to the market.

questions.explanation: The subject forms are I, we, you, he, she, it, they: 'He is going to the market.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct object form?

options.A: The teacher praised he.

questions.explanation: The object forms are me, us, you, him, her, it, them: 'The teacher praised him.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a possessive pronoun correctly?

options.A: This book is mine.

questions.explanation: Possessive pronouns show ownership and stand independently: mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs. Example: 'This book is mine.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a demonstrative pronoun correctly?

options.A: These are expensive.

questions.explanation: This and that are singular; these and those are plural: 'These are expensive.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses an interrogative pronoun correctly?

options.A: Who called you?

questions.explanation: Who is the subject form used to ask a question: 'Who called you?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a relative pronoun correctly?

options.A: The woman who won the prize is my teacher.
options.B: The woman whom won the prize is my teacher.
options.C: The woman whose won the prize is my teacher.
options.D: The woman which won the prize is my teacher.

questions.explanation: Who generally refers to people and functions as the subject of the relative clause: 'The woman who won the prize is my teacher.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'whose' correctly as a relative pronoun?

options.A: The student whose bag was missing reported it.
options.B: The student who bag was missing reported it.
options.C: The student whom bag was missing reported it.
options.D: The student which bag was missing reported it.

questions.explanation: Whose expresses possession and can refer to people: 'The student whose bag was missing reported it.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses 'which' correctly as a relative pronoun?

options.A: The book which I bought is interesting.
options.B: The book who I bought is interesting.
options.C: The book whom I bought is interesting.
options.D: The book whose I bought is interesting.

questions.explanation: Which generally refers to animals or things: 'The book which I bought is interesting.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a reciprocal pronoun correctly?

options.A: The two friends help each other.
options.C: The two friends help each others.
options.D: The two friends help one others.

questions.explanation: A reciprocal pronoun expresses a mutual relationship: each other and one another: 'The two friends help each other.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a substitute or prop pronoun correctly?

options.A: I prefer the red shirt; do you have one?
options.B: I prefer the red shirt; do you have it one?
options.C: I prefer the red shirt; do you have ones?
options.D: I prefer the red shirt; do you have the one?

questions.explanation: A substitute pronoun stands in place of a previously mentioned noun or noun phrase, preventing repetition: 'I prefer the red shirt; do you have one?'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a linking verb?

options.A: The soup tastes delicious.

questions.explanation: A linking verb connects the subject to a subject complement that describes or identifies it: 'The soup tastes delicious.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a phrasal verb correctly?

options.A: She gave up smoking.

questions.explanation: A phrasal verb is a combination of a verb and one or more particles that functions as a unit: give up (quit): 'She gave up smoking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a modal auxiliary correctly?

options.A: She can sing.

questions.explanation: A modal auxiliary is followed by the base form of the verb: 'She can sing.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence shows correct agreement with 'either...or' when the nearer subject is singular?

options.A: Either the workers or the manager is coming.
options.B: Either the workers or the manager are coming.
options.C: Either the workers or the manager were coming.
options.D: Either the workers or the manager have coming.

questions.explanation: When either...or joins two subjects, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject: 'Either the workers or the manager is coming.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses an attributive adjective?

options.A: a beautiful garden

questions.explanation: An attributive adjective appears before the noun it modifies: 'a beautiful garden.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a predicative adjective?

options.A: a beautiful garden

questions.explanation: A predicative adjective appears after a linking verb and describes the subject: 'The garden is beautiful.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence uses a postpositive adjective?

options.A: a beautiful garden

questions.explanation: A postpositive adjective follows the noun or pronoun it modifies, often in fixed expressions or formal usage: 'something useful'; 'the people responsible.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'hard' and 'hardly'?

options.A: Hard means with effort or intensity; hardly means almost not
options.B: Hard means almost not; hardly means with effort

questions.explanation: Hard means with effort or intensity; hardly means almost not. 'He works hard' differs from 'He hardly works.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between 'late' and 'lately'?

options.A: Late means after the expected time; lately means recently
options.B: Late means recently; lately means after the expected time
options.D: Both mean after the expected time

questions.explanation: Late means after the expected time; lately means recently.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'beside'?

options.A: She sat beside me.

questions.explanation: Beside means next to: 'She sat beside me.' Besides means in addition to or apart from.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'besides'?

options.A: She sat besides me.
options.D: Besides of English, she speaks Kannada.

questions.explanation: Besides means in addition to or apart from: 'Besides English, she speaks Kannada.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'into'?

options.A: The child is into the room.
options.B: The child ran into the room.
options.C: The child ran in the room.
options.D: The child is into the room now.

questions.explanation: In commonly indicates position; into indicates movement from outside to inside: 'The child ran into the room.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'onto'?

options.A: The book is onto the desk.
options.B: Put the book onto the desk.
options.C: Put the book on the desk.
options.D: Put the book in the desk.

questions.explanation: On commonly indicates position; onto indicates movement to a surface: 'Put the book onto the desk.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'not only...but also'?

options.A: She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
options.B: She is not only intelligent but also hardwork.
options.C: She is not only intelligence but also hardworking.
options.D: She is not only intelligent but also hardworks.

questions.explanation: Parallelism with correlative conjunctions requires balanced grammatical forms: 'She is not only intelligent but also hardworking.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'whether...or'?

options.A: I don't know whether he will come or not.
options.B: I don't know whether he will come and not.
options.C: I don't know whether he will come but not.
options.D: I don't know whether he will come so not.

questions.explanation: Whether...or is a pair of correlative conjunctions: 'I don't know whether he will come or not.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'rather...than'?

options.A: I would rather read than watch TV.
options.B: I would rather read than watching TV.
options.C: I would rather reading than watch TV.
options.D: I would rather to read than to watch TV.

questions.explanation: Rather...than is a pair of correlative conjunctions: 'I would rather read than watch TV.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with a superlative adjective?

options.A: She is the most useful book author.
options.B: She is most useful book author.
options.C: She is a most useful book author.
options.D: She is an most useful book author.

questions.explanation: Use the before a superlative adjective in ordinary attributive use: the tallest building, the most useful book.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'the' with a unique entity?

options.A: The Moon is bright tonight.

questions.explanation: Use the with entities understood as unique in the context: the Sun, the Moon, the Earth, the sky.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: He is angry about the situation.
options.B: He is angry with the situation only.
options.C: He is angry to the situation.
options.D: He is angry of the situation.

questions.explanation: Angry about or at can refer to a situation or matter: 'He is angry about the situation.' Angry with is used when referring to a person.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: She is good at mathematics.

questions.explanation: Good at is used for skill: 'She is good at mathematics.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: Success depends in effort.

questions.explanation: Depend on/upon: 'Success depends on effort.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: She is married with a doctor.
options.B: She is married to a doctor.
options.C: She is married at a doctor.
options.D: She is married for a doctor.

questions.explanation: Married to: 'She is married to a doctor.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The child is afraid from dogs.
options.B: The child is afraid of dogs.
options.C: The child is afraid at dogs.
options.D: The child is afraid with dogs.

questions.explanation: Afraid of: 'The child is afraid of dogs.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: The team consists in eleven players.
options.B: The team consists of eleven players.
options.C: The team consists at eleven players.
options.D: The team consists with eleven players.

questions.explanation: Consist of: 'The team consists of eleven players.'

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the correct expression?

options.A: This book belongs in me.

questions.explanation: Belong to: 'This book belongs to me.'
